| Independently, run-with-timeout (`run(timeout)`, whose timeout is the caller's run budget named in [EXEC-041]; its expiry fails the caller's wait and does not by itself end the run) MAY expose a policy for what happens to the loop when the caller's timeout expires: *abandon* (leave the loop running; the historical default, rarely desirable) or *close* (stop it per [ENV-013]).<br><br>The expiry of the caller's timeout MUST NOT complete the loop's own result: an abandoned loop can still report its real final marking.<br><br>*Where* an implementation exposes this policy, *when* the caller's timeout expires while the loop is running, the implementation *shall* act on the expiry under the policy the caller chose.<br><br>*When* the caller's timeout expires under *abandon*, the implementation *shall* leave the executor as it was, including its marking, its lifecycle mode, its queues, its firings in flight and the position of its loop, and a running loop *shall* go on running.<br><br>*When* the caller's timeout expires under *close* while the executor is open or draining, the implementation *shall* close the executor as a call of `close()` does ([ENV-013]), even while its loop is running.<br><br>*When* the caller's timeout expires under *close* after the executor is already closed or stopped, the implementation *shall* leave the executor as it was.<br><br>*When* the caller's timeout expires while the loop is running, the implementation *shall not* end the run and *shall not* change the marking.<br><br>Under a *close* policy the executor is closed on timeout and the loop then stops as [ENV-013] says, once its in-flight actions complete; under *abandon* it keeps running. | 1. For every executor R, every expiry handling X of its run-with-timeout and every configuration C:<br>2. an expiry under abandon from state s ends in s itself;<br>3. an expiry under close from a state s whose mode is open or draining ends in a state that a close step of R reaches from s, and from a state s whose mode is closed or stopped it ends in s itself;<br>4. an expiry from a state in which the loop is running ends in a state in which the loop is still running, with the same marking. | <pre>fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] R X ↦<br>  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),<br>    (on fun s s' ↦ X C TimeoutPolicy.abandon s s', shall fun s s' ↦ s' = s) ∧<br>      (on fun s s' ↦ X C TimeoutPolicy.close s s', shall fun s s' ↦<br>          (s.mode = Mode.open ∨ s.mode = Mode.draining → R C s XLbl.close s') ∧<br>            (s.mode = Mode.closed ∨ s.mode = Mode.stopped → s' = s)) ∧<br>        ∀ (pol : TimeoutPolicy),<br>          on fun s s' ↦ X C pol s s' ∧ isExecPhase s.phase = true, shall fun s s' ↦<br>            isExecPhase s'.phase = true ∧ s'.M = s.M</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is a pair: an executor R : XRel N T (glossary GlossaryExec.lean), where R C s l s' says that under configuration C the step labelled l leads from executor state s to s', and the expiry handling X : ExpiryRel N T of its run-with-timeout, where X C pol s s' says that the expiry of the caller's timeout under policy pol (TimeoutPolicy: abandon or close) takes the executor from s to s'. The expiry is an event of the host's clock, which the model does not carry (ruling D18 (b)), so it is a relation beside R and not a label of XLbl. The caller's own result (Java's returned stage failing with a TimeoutException, TypeScript's rejected promise) is not executor state and is outside the model. The witnesses are the reference executor RefExec (Reference/Exec.lean) and refExpiry: abandon changes nothing, close is RefExec's close step, or nothing when the executor is already closed or stopped.
- That the expiry is handled under the policy the caller chose, and not another, is the meaning of X's policy argument: X C pol s s' is the handling of a run whose caller chose pol, so lines 1 and 2 say what each choice does, and the coverage clause Env016Covers says that the handling takes effect at all. The binding of the caller's argument to pol is not modelled further; an implementation that swapped the two policies breaks line 1 on the abandon side (ENV_016_forbids_abandonCloses) and line 2 on the close side (ENV_016_forbids_closeIgnored).
- Scope (Status Proposed, priority MAY, ruling D47 (c)): the block applies to the implementations that expose the policy, Java (run(Duration, RunTimeoutPolicy) in BitmapNetExecutor and PrecompiledNetExecutor) and TypeScript (run(timeoutMs, onTimeout) in both executors). Rust and Python have no run-with-timeout policy. Java's PetriNetExecutor interface has a default run(timeout, policy) that ignores the policy and abandons: an executor that keeps that default does not provide the close policy, and one that claimed to would break line 2 (ENV_016_forbids_closeIgnored).
- Its offer is in ExecCoversW5.Env016Covers (ConsistencyExec.lean; the convention of GlossaryExec.lean: offers are coverage clauses, never block lines). The third EARS sentence demands an answer and is quoted whole; its safety halves are lines 1 and 2, and its existence half is that clause: from every state in which the loop is running, an expiry under either policy has an outcome in X, which the reference meets (env016_ref_covers). AC3 is lines 1 to 3 with that clause. Under abandon the expiry changes nothing and the loop keeps running (line 1; ENV_016_forbids_abandonCloses: an expiry that closes the executor under abandon breaks it). Under close, from an open or draining executor, the expiry is the executor's own close step (line 2; ENV_016_forbids_closeIgnored: an expiry that leaves the executor open breaks it, and so does ENV_016_forbids_closeTerminates, an expiry that stops the loop without waiting for its firings in flight, as terminateNow does under ENV-015). Line 2 reads 'already closed or stopped' on the lifecycle mode, not on the steps R offers, so line 2 and Env016Covers together require R to have a close step from every open or draining state in which its loop runs: an executor that refuses close() while its loop runs, so that the close policy acts as abandon, breaks line 2 (ENV_016_forbids_closeRefusedWhileRunning), and an expiry handling that gave such an executor no outcome there instead would fail Env016Covers. The expiry under close does not stop the loop at once (line 3; ENV_016_forbids_closeFinishes). That the loop then stops once its in-flight actions complete is ENV-013's requirement (its item 4), not a line of this block; ENV_016_nonvacuous part 3 shows it on the test derivation's run. Env016Covers makes the expiry take effect at all: an implementation whose expiry handler never runs meets every line and fails the clause (env016_covers_unhandled). The clause asks for an outcome only while the loop runs: once the run has returned, Java's orTimeout and TypeScript's cleared timer no longer fire.
- The MUST NOT sentence is line 3 with line 1: no expiry while the loop runs ends the run or changes the marking, so the result the loop reports, the marking at its finish and the fact that it ended (EXEC-041), is fixed only by a finish step of the loop. Line 3 adds to line 1 only under close, where it constrains R's own close step; under abandon it follows from line 1. An implementation whose timer completes the loop's own result with the marking at the expiry, the defect Java's loop.copy() avoids, breaks line 1 (ENV_016_forbids_expiryCompletes); one whose close finishes the run at once, reporting the marking at the expiry, breaks line 3 although its expiry is its own close step (ENV_016_forbids_closeFinishes). 'An abandoned loop can still report its real final marking' is ENV_016_nonvacuous part 2: after an expiry under abandon the action in flight returns, its output is deposited, and the loop finishes quiescent with that output in the marking it reports.
- The termination reason an abandoned run reports is EXEC-041's question, not this block's (env-b ENVB-R6 (a), ruling D53 (c)): TypeScript sets its reason to stopped when the caller's timeout expires and keeps it if the loop later ends on its own. That field is reporting state outside the executor state of the model, and D53 (c) allows it, since stopped is not a completed reason. Lines 1 and 3 speak of the executor state and the marking only.
- Java closes the executor from a callback that runs after the returned stage has failed (whenCompleteAsync), so loop steps may come between the expiry and the close. The model places the expiry at the moment close() takes effect; a run in which loop steps come first is a run of R whose close step comes later. TypeScript calls close() in the turn that rejects the promise.
- Which policy is the default is configuration (kind N) and not a line: run(timeout) without a policy abandons in Java and TypeScript, the historical default of the text. The lines hold for whichever policy the caller chooses.
- AC1, AC2 and the first paragraph are the second block of ENV-016, ENV_016_await (ENV_016_l1.lean, wave W7, ruling D47 (c)), over the event model RefEvents, since the answer waits for the step that emits ExecutionCompleted: awaitTermination answers true when the loop was never started, false while it runs, true only after the finish step that answers the queued inject() calls and only once no emission of ExecutionCompleted is still to come, and true once the loop has finished, whatever a failing event store did. Blocking, the timeout of awaitTermination and 'promptly' are kind Q.
- The test derivation (a net with an action still in flight when a short timeout expires, under each policy; the executor closed under close and the loop stopping once the action completes, the loop still live under abandon and reporting the action's output) is ENV_016_nonvacuous: at the expiry the loop is still running, parked with a firing in flight; under close the executor is closed by R's close step and the loop finishes closed after the action completes; under abandon the executor is unchanged and the loop goes on to finish quiescent with the action's output. The awaitTermination half of the test derivation is ENV_016_await_nonvacuous, on the same run.

## ENV-016: Observable Termination (awaitTermination)

`Libpetri.Spec.ENV_016_await` · Kind **B** · Scope executors that provide awaitTermination (Java: BitmapNetExecutor and PrecompiledNetExecutor), for the first run of an executor · Source **verbatim** (spec/06-environment-places.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 faa6050b43b2a37d ai** · Statement hash `faa6050b43b2a37d`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| An implementation MAY provide `awaitTermination(timeout)`, which blocks until the orchestrator loop has finished its termination bookkeeping (pending `inject()` futures completed, `ExecutionCompleted` emitted), returning whether termination was observed within the timeout.<br><br>It returns promptly when the loop was never started, and it MUST NOT itself be defeated by a failure in that bookkeeping (for example a throwing event store).<br><br>*Where* an implementation provides `awaitTermination`, *when* it is called on an executor whose loop was never started, the implementation *shall* answer true at once, without waiting for the timeout.<br><br>*Where* an implementation provides `awaitTermination`, *when* it is called on an executor whose loop has started, the implementation *shall* wait until the loop has finished its termination bookkeeping or the timeout has expired, whichever comes first.<br><br>*Where* an implementation provides `awaitTermination`, *when* its wait ends while the loop is still running, the implementation *shall* answer false.<br><br>*Where* an implementation provides `awaitTermination`, the implementation *shall not* answer true for a run before the loop has taken the step that ends the run and, in that step, answered every accepted `inject()` still pending.<br><br>*Where* an implementation provides `awaitTermination`, the implementation *shall not* answer true for a run while the emission of `ExecutionCompleted` ([EVT-003]) for that run is still to come.<br><br>*Where* an implementation provides `awaitTermination`, **Assumptions**

- The model is a pair: an executor with events E : EvExec N T (Reference/Events.lean), whose steps E.step C H s l evs s' append the events evs, and the answer relation A : AwaitRel N T of its awaitTermination. A C none b says that on an executor whose loop was never started the call answers b; A C (some (H, s)) b says that when the wait ends at a point of a run (RunAt: a labelled run of E from the initial state, H everything it emitted, s the state it reached) the call answers b. The call reads and changes nothing: A is not a step of E. The witnesses are refEvExec (under both emission variants) and refAwait, which answers true when the loop was never started and otherwise whether the loop has finished.
- The wait itself is kind Q and not modelled: the sentence that the call waits until the loop has finished its termination bookkeeping or the timeout has expired, whichever comes first, 'blocks until' and 'within the timeout' of the first quoted sentence, and 'promptly' and 'at once, without waiting for the timeout' of the sentences on a loop that never started. The model places the answer at the moment the wait ends, a point of the run, so a run that finishes during the wait is answered at its finished state. An implementation that polls without waiting meets every line; one that waits out its timeout on a loop that never started and then answers true meets line 1.
- The termination bookkeeping is the finish step of the model: the step finish c enters the finished phase, answers every accepted event still queued (eq becomes empty: Java completes those inject() futures with false in drainPendingExternalEvents) and emits ExecutionCompleted (EVT-003) when the store accepts it. Java does the same work in the finally block of its loop and completes the future awaitTermination waits on last (BitmapNetExecutor.java 1077-1125, PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 1887-1938).
- Line 1 is AC2 and the sentence on a loop that never started: an implementation that waits out its timeout on a loop that never started and answers false breaks it (ENV_016_await_mutant_blocksUnstarted, which keeps lines 2 to 5). A rejected start is a loop that never started: when the submit of Java's run(Duration) is rejected, as on an executor whose own pool an earlier close() shut down or on a caller-supplied executor that rejects the task, run puts started back to its previous value before it rethrows, so the call answers true at once. A started flag left set over a loop that never runs makes the call wait out its timeout and answer false, the behaviour ENV_016_await_mutant_blocksUnstarted models, which RD-34 (a) in spec/runtime-defects.md recorded.
- Lines 2 and 5 are AC1: false while the loop is still running, true once it has stopped. The default method of Java's PetriNetExecutor interface answers true always, so an executor that kept it would break line 2 (ENV_016_await_forbids_alwaysTrue), and line 3 with it: on an executor that never leaves a finished phase (EXEC-041) an answer true while the loop runs has no finish step behind it, so line 2 has no mutant that keeps every other line; BitmapNetExecutor and PrecompiledNetExecutor override it.
- Lines 3 and 4 are the first quoted sentence, 'blocks until the orchestrator loop has finished its termination bookkeeping (pending inject() futures completed, ExecutionCompleted emitted)'. Line 3: an answer true needs a finish step in the run that left no accepted event queued. An executor whose loop ends before it answers the events still queued breaks it (ENV_016_await_mutant_lateDrain, which keeps lines 1, 2, 4 and 5), and so does one whose close ends the run without the finish step, so that its caller is told the loop terminated although no ExecutionCompleted was ever emitted (ENV_016_await_forbids_closeEnds). Line 3 reads the queue in the finish step, not at the point of the answer: an inject() that queues its event after the loop has finished breaks the inject() requirements (ENV-003, ENV-013), not this block (ENV_016_await_allows_lateInject).
- Line 4: an answer true needs the emission of ExecutionCompleted to be over, so no later step of the run emits it. An executor that completes the future the call waits on before it emits ExecutionCompleted, which a later step then appends, breaks it although its store never fails (ENV_016_await_mutant_lateCompleted, which keeps lines 1, 2, 3 and 5). Line 4 does not ask that ExecutionCompleted is in H: a store that throws on it never receives it, and line 4 then holds since nothing of it is still to come.
- Line 5 is 'MUST NOT itself be defeated by a failure in that bookkeeping' for the answer: once the loop has finished the answer is true. A store that throws when the termination events are appended is modelled as an executor whose finish step appends nothing, since the events never reach the store (in Java a throwing snapshot append skips ExecutionCompleted too, BitmapNetExecutor.java 1091-1116). The reference answer reads the state only, so it meets the block over that executor as well (ENV_016_await_allows_throwingStore), while an answer that waits for ExecutionCompleted to reach the store answers false for ever and breaks line 5 (ENV_016_await_mutant_waitsForStore, which keeps lines 1 to 4). A failure before the first cycle has no step of its own in the model, which has no step for a loop that dies before its run. Java emits ExecutionStarted and the first marking snapshot inside the try/finally of its loop (BitmapNetExecutor.java 1018-1029, PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 1830-1841), so a store that throws on them ends the loop through the same finally, which sets the termination reason (stopped, unless a marked terminal place or an earlier close decides it), answers the queued events and completes the future the call waits on: the run ends with a finish step whose events never reach the store, as in ENV_016_await_allows_throwingStore, and the call answers true once the loop has stopped (AC1). A loop that dies there without the finish step and without completing that future, the behaviour RD-34 (b) in spec/runtime-defects.md recorded, reads in the model as a loop that stays running: it meets every line but breaks AC1 and the quoted 'MUST NOT itself be defeated by a failure in that bookkeeping (for example a throwing event store)', so AC1 is tested for it (AbstractNetExecutorEnvironmentTest awaitTermination_trueAfterABootThatThrew_ENV016_AC1), not proven.
- That the call returns at all is an offer and so no line: the sentence that a failure in the termination bookkeeping shall not keep the call from returning its answer, and 'returning whether termination was observed', are the coverage clause Env016AwaitCovers (every call has an answer), which the consistency theorem takes with the block. An implementation whose call never returns or raises meets every line and fails it (env016_await_covers_hang). The clause asks an answer at every argument, unreachable states included, which is more than the sentence needs and which the reference meets.
- Lines 3 to 5 also bound the executor, not only its answer: at a finished point line 5 asks true, so the run must have taken a finish step that answered the queue and must emit no ExecutionCompleted later. This restates for awaitTermination what EXEC-041 ('end a run only by finishing it'), ENV-013 (a closed executor ends its run with no external event queued) and EVT-003 already ask of the loop.
- Scope (Status Proposed, priority MAY, ruling D47 (c)): only Java provides awaitTermination, in BitmapNetExecutor and PrecompiledNetExecutor. TypeScript provides the run-timeout policy of the first block but not awaitTermination; Rust and Python provide neither. The run-timeout policy and the third paragraph's EARS sentences are the first block of ENV-016, ENV_016 (ENV_016.lean); AC3 is that block's.
- One run per executor, as the quoted scope sentence says: a point of a run starts from the initial state. Whether an executor may run again is not specified. Java does not refuse a second run(), and its termination future is completed once, so on a second run of the same executor its awaitTermination answers true while the second loop runs; that is outside this block and is no runtime defect while the spec leaves a second run open.
- The test derivation (awaitTermination reports the transition of a run whose action is still in flight when a short timeout expires) is ENV_016_await_nonvacuous on the first block's run: while the action is in flight the loop is running and the answer is false; after the close of the timeout policy, the action's return and the closed finish, the answer is true, the finish step left no accepted event queued and the run has emitted ExecutionCompleted. A call before the run answers true.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-EVT_002"></a>
## EVT-002: ExecutionStarted Event

`Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002` · Kind **B** · Scope all executors (event store enabled) · Source **verbatim** (spec/08-events-observability.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 c3022e6f56a846eb ai** · Statement hash `c3022e6f56a846eb`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *When* a run starts, the executor *shall* emit an ExecutionStarted event before its first cycle ([EXEC-001]) and before any event of the run other than a log message ([EVT-013]).<br><br>The executor *shall* emit at most one ExecutionStarted event per run. | 1. For every executor with events E, every configuration C, every initial marking M0, every initial reading r0 and every event trace tr of a run of E from M0 at r0 (the events the run emits before its first step, then the events of each step):<br>2. tr contains an ExecutionStarted event;<br>3. tr contains at most one ExecutionStarted event;<br>4. every event of tr before its first ExecutionStarted event is a log message. | <pre>fun {N T} E ↦<br>  ∀ (C : Cfg N T) (M0 : QMarking N T) (r0 : ℕ) (tr : List (NetEvent N T)),<br>    Trace E C M0 r0 tr →<br>      (occurs fun e ↦ e.kind == NetEventKind.executionStarted) tr ∧<br>        (at-most-once fun e ↦ e.kind == NetEventKind.executionStarted) tr ∧<br>          (until fun e ↦ e.kind == NetEventKind.executionStarted, never fun e ↦<br>              !e.isLog &amp;&amp; e.kind != NetEventKind.executionStarted)<br>            tr</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is an executor with events E : EvExec N T (Reference/Events.lean): the events a run emits before its first step (its boot) and a step relation that says which events each step appends. Trace E C M0 r0 tr says that tr is what E emits on some run from the initial state of M0: the boot events, then the events of each step, in order. A trace is a finite prefix of a run and the empty run is a run, so every line holds after every step, and the boot events alone are a trace. The first cycle of the run (EXEC-001) begins with its first step, so 'before its first cycle' in the first quoted sentence reads as 'among the boot events': an executor that emits ExecutionStarted only inside its first step breaks line 1 on the boot-only trace, even when that step emits nothing else. The witness is the reference executor with events refEvExec, under both emission variants (polJT for Java and TypeScript, polRust for Rust and Python): its boot is ExecutionStarted, then (Java and TypeScript) the snapshot of the initial marking, and no step emits an ExecutionStarted. refEvExec_erase (Reference/EventsLink.lean) shows that it steps exactly as RefExec, so the block constrains what is emitted and nothing else.
- Line 1 and line 3 are the first quoted sentence: the run announces itself, and no event other than a log message comes first. An executor that announces nothing at all breaks line 1 and keeps lines 2 and 3 (EVT_002_mutant_silent); one that publishes the snapshot of the initial marking before ExecutionStarted breaks line 3 (EVT_002_mutant_snapshotFirst). Line 2 is the second quoted sentence: an executor that announces the run again each time it wakes from a wait breaks it (EVT_002_mutant_wakeAgain). AC1 (emitted exactly once per execution run, before any transitions fire) is lines 1 and 2 (exactly once) and line 3 (TransitionStarted is not a log message, so it comes after).
- A run is one call that runs the executor: a second run of the same executor is a run of its own, with its own boot and its own ExecutionStarted, and the lines read each run's trace from its boot. Java and TypeScript emit ExecutionStarted first in their run loop (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/BitmapNetExecutor.java 1004-1005, PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 1834-1835; typescript/src/runtime/bitmap-net-executor.ts 524-529, precompiled-net-executor.ts 584-589), Rust at the top of run_sync and of the asynchronous run (rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor_core/executor.rs 374-377 and 1012-1015), which Python runs on. No runtime emits it anywhere else.
- Log messages before ExecutionStarted are allowed, and where they fall is not fixed (ruling D20; design note SC-3): Java and TypeScript report unknown initial places and dead arcs at construction, before the run (BitmapNetExecutor.java 834-835, bitmap-net-executor.ts 401-410); Rust reports dead arcs at construction and the unknown initial places right after ExecutionStarted (executor_core/executor.rs 379 and 1017). An executor whose boot puts a construction diagnostic first meets the block (EVT_002_allows_diagnosticsFirst). The reference emits no diagnostic yet (Reference/Events.lean).
- The payload is not modelled (ruling D38 (a)): the timestamp (the epoch clock is the CORE-011 slice) and the net name, which every runtime's event carries (the net of the model has no name), are listed in the markdown without a shall sentence, so no block states them. The execution ID: Java and TypeScript events carry it and Rust and Python events do not (executor_core/executor.rs 84-88: the ID exists, kept off the events so as not to change the session archive format, EVT-025). Distinctness of the ID (AC2) is the second block of EVT-002, EVT_002_executionId; the ID on the ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted events (the sentence on the lifecycle events) is the third, EVT_002_lifecycleId. The event model of this block (NetEvent in Spec/GlossaryEvents.lean) carries no ID, so an executor that puts a wrong ID on its events meets this block and breaks the third.
- Assumptions shared by the executor event blocks: the event store is enabled and its append does not fail (EVT-020, cited by the markdown sentence that a run's events reach the event store only while the store is enabled; Java's PrecompiledNetExecutor and Rust emit only when the store is enabled, so a run with a noop store that emits nothing is no breach); an event is a value (EVT-001); transition names are distinct (ruling D10). The events of one step are contiguous in the model, since a step appends its events at once. Java appends ActionTimedOut events and the log messages it captures from actions from other threads than the orchestrator (the timeout callback BitmapNetExecutor.fireTransition hands java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/ExecutorSupport.java withActionTimeout, which appends through emitEvent from the timer thread; LogCaptureScope.java wrapRunnable and wrapCallable), so in a Java store such an event can fall between the events of one step; the lines are read on the store with those events left out, as the reading at the top of spec/08-events-observability.md says. TypeScript and Rust append every event from the orchestrator.
- The test derivation (run the net, verify the first event other than a log message is ExecutionStarted with the correct net name) is EVT_002_nonvacuous without the net name: a run that enables and starts a transition emits ExecutionStarted first, exactly once, and the TransitionStarted after it. The net-name check is a runtime test only, for the payload reason above.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✓ The reference executor with the Java and TypeScript emission meets EVT-002: a run first announces itself with `ExecutionStarted`, then publishes the snapshot of the initial marking, and no step announces the run again.
  <pre>∀ {N T : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N] [inst_1 : Ord N], EVT_002 (refEvExec polJT)</pre>
- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_rust` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✓ The reference executor with the Rust and Python emission meets EVT-002 too: its boot is the `ExecutionStarted` alone.
  <pre>∀ {N T : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N] [inst_1 : Ord N], EVT_002 (refEvExec polRust)</pre>
- ✓ **allows** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_allows_diagnosticsFirst` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✓ A log message before `ExecutionStarted` is allowed: an executor that reports an unknown initial place when it is constructed, as Java and TypeScript do, and only then announces the run, meets EVT-002.
  <pre>EVT_002 evt002_diagFirst</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_mutant_silent` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✗ A run that announces nothing violates EVT-002 (line 1): an executor that emits no event at all, at the boot or at any step, has emitted nothing when it is booted, so its trace holds no `ExecutionStarted`. With no event at all, nothing is announced twice and nothing comes before an announcement, so it keeps lines 2 and 3.
  <pre>evt002_lines23 evt002_mute ∧ ¬EVT_002 evt002_mute</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_mutant_snapshotFirst` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✗ Publishing the initial marking before announcing the run violates EVT-002 (line 3): with the token 7 in place 0, the boot emits the snapshot of place 0 first and `ExecutionStarted` second, and a snapshot is not a log message. <a id="Libpetri-Spec-EVT_002_executionId"></a>
## EVT-002: ExecutionStarted Event (execution ID)

`Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_executionId` · Kind **F** · Scope Java, TypeScript and Rust executors · Source **verbatim** (spec/08-events-observability.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 69458457038bd34e ai** · Statement hash `69458457038bd34e`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| Two executors constructed in one process from the same copy of the library *shall* carry different execution IDs, whatever the clock reads when each is constructed ([TIME-015] AC14). | 1. For every execution ID assignment ids, where ids k r is the execution ID of the executor constructed k-th in its process from one copy of the library while the clock reads r: two executors constructed at different places k and k' in the construction order carry different IDs, for all clock readings r and r'. | <pre>fun ids ↦ ∀ (k k' r r' : ℕ), k ≠ k' → ids k r ≠ ids k' r'</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- This is the second block of EVT-002 (ruling D98 (a)): the ID identifies the executor, and its distinctness is the MUST half of TIME-015 AC14, which no other block states (TIME-015 points AC14 at this block). The model is the assignment ids : Nat → Nat → String: the ID depends on the executor's place k in the process's construction order and, in a wrong implementation, on the clock reading r at construction. All runtimes draw the ID at construction from one counter per copy of the library shared by both executors (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/ExecutorSupport.java 39-40 and 111-113, used by BitmapNetExecutor.java 169 and PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 290; typescript/src/runtime/executor-support.ts 82-102, used by bitmap-net-executor.ts 187 and precompiled-net-executor.ts 172; rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor_core/executor.rs 48 and 164-165), so k counts the executors of both kinds. The witness refExecutionId is that counter in lower-case hex. An implementation that takes the ID from the clock reading, as TypeScript did before AC14 (executor-support.ts 86-91), separates executors constructed at different readings and breaks the line under an injected clock that reads the same twice (EVT_002_executionId_mutant_clock).
- Out of scope: a counter that wraps (2 to the 64 constructions in Java and Rust; TypeScript numbers stay exact up to 2 to the 53), executors in different processes (a per-process counter restarts at 0, which AC14 does not ask to avoid), executors constructed from different copies of the library in one process, each with its own counter that starts at 0 (a TypeScript module instance per worker thread or realm, executor-support.ts 82 and 100-102; a Java class loaded by two class loaders, ExecutorSupport.java 111-113; two instances of the Rust crate), and reproducibility, the SHOULD half of AC14 (refExecutionId does not read the clock, so a replay with the same construction order gets the same IDs, EVT_002_executionId_nonvacuous). Whether the ID is on the events is the third block, EVT_002_lifecycleId: Java and TypeScript put it on ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted, Rust and Python do not.
- The model is a restriction: the ID is a function of the construction place k and the clock reading r and of nothing else, so an ID drawn from randomness, a thread or the net cannot be written as an assignment, and the block separates the counter from a clock-derived ID only. No runtime draws the ID from anything but the counter. Python is out of scope: the binding constructs Rust executors, which draw from the Rust counter, but it exposes no execution ID (no execution_id in rust/libpetri-py/src), so from Python the line cannot be observed; Rust exposes it through the pub fn execution_id (executor_core/executor.rs 285-286) and not on events.
- AC2 (two executors constructed in one process carry different execution IDs, even at the same clock reading) is the line. The text before ruling D98 asked for an ID unique across runs: one executor can run more than once and keeps its ID, so no runtime has a per-run ID.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_executionId_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✓ The reference execution ID meets the block: the counter is read in hex, and two counter values never print the same.
  <pre>EVT_002_executionId refExecutionId</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_executionId_mutant_clock` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✗ Taking the ID from the clock reading violates the block: under an injected clock that reads 3 at both constructions, the first two executors both get "3". Such an ID still separates executors constructed at different readings.
  <pre>evt002_apartAcrossReadings evt002ClockId ∧ ¬EVT_002_executionId evt002ClockId</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_executionId_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✓ The block is exercised by the reference: the first two executors constructed while the clock reads 5 get the IDs "0" and "1"; the 27th gets "1a" whatever the clock reads, so a replay in the same construction order gets the same IDs.
  <pre>refExecutionId 0 5 = "0" ∧<br>  refExecutionId 1 5 = "1" ∧ refExecutionId 26 0 = "1a" ∧ refExecutionId 26 9 = "1a"</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.joint_events_exec_sketch` (Libpetri.Spec.ConsistencyEvents): ✓ The executor part of the event requirements: the one executor every execution block of wave W5 holds of (with its validator, expiry handling, queue firing and timed step), and an executor with events that steps exactly as it and meets every executor event block, with the action log and the `awaitTermination` answer it offers; over string place names the same executor also meets EVT-014; beside them, the execution IDs, the lifecycle IDs and the run duration. For example, a run that fires one transition and quiesces emits `ExecutionStarted` first and `ExecutionCompleted` last, once each, every token a start takes is reported by one `TokenRemoved` event of its place, and with places declared as `b`, `c`, `a` the marking at the start is reported as `a` then `b`.
  <pre>∀ {N T : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N],<br>  (∃ V E X Q R W A Aw, ExecSpec V E X Q R ∧ W.erase = E ∧ EventsSpec W A Aw) ∧<br>    (∃ V E X Q R W A Aw,<br>        ExecSpec V E X Q R ∧ W.erase = E ∧ EventsSpec W A Aw ∧ EVT_014 W) ∧<br>      (∃ ids, EVT_002_executionId ids) ∧<br>        (∃ L, EVT_002_lifecycleId L) ∧ ∃ d, EVT_003_duration d</pre>

## EVT-002: ExecutionStarted Event (execution ID on the lifecycle events)

`Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_lifecycleId` · Kind **F** · Scope Java and TypeScript executors (the lifecycle events of Rust and Python carry no execution ID) · Source **verbatim** (spec/08-events-observability.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 8898a843f9ad8d20 ai** · Statement hash `8898a843f9ad8d20`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *Where* the lifecycle events carry the execution ID (Java and TypeScript), the ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted events of every run *shall* carry the ID of the executor that runs it. | 1. For every observation L of the execution IDs, where L.exec k r is the ID of the executor constructed k-th in its process while the clock reads r, and L.onStarted k r j and L.onCompleted k r j are the IDs on the ExecutionStarted and ExecutionCompleted events of its j-th run: for all k, r and j,<br>2. the ExecutionStarted event of the run carries the executor's ID, L.onStarted k r j = L.exec k r;<br>3. the ExecutionCompleted event of the run carries the executor's ID, L.onCompleted k r j = L.exec k r. | <pre>fun L ↦ ∀ (k r j : ℕ), L.onStarted k r j = L.exec k r ∧ L.onCompleted k r j = L.exec k r</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- This is the third block of EVT-002 and the Java and TypeScript companion of ruling D98 (a): the event model of the first block (NetEvent in Spec/GlossaryEvents.lean) carries no execution ID, so this block states the ID on the events over what a host observes, the executor's executionId() and the ID field of each lifecycle event, and needs no new field on NetEvent. The model is Evt002LifeIds, indexed by the executor (its place k in the construction order and the reading r at construction, as in EVT_002_executionId) and the run j, so every run of one executor carries the same ID and both events of one run carry the same ID. The witness refLifecycleIds builds both events from executionId(), as both Java executors and both TypeScript executors do.
- Each line has its own wrong observation. An executor that draws a fresh ID from the shared counter for its ExecutionStarted event (TypeScript nextExecutionId() in executor-support.ts 100-102 in place of this.executionId()) gives the first executor the ID 0 and its event the ID 1; its executor IDs stay distinct, so it meets the first two blocks and breaks line 1 (EVT_002_lifecycleId_mutant_freshDraw). An executor that puts its ν execution scope (NU-011, a random token drawn per executor and not the execution ID, BitmapNetExecutor.java 790-793) on its ExecutionCompleted event breaks line 2 (EVT_002_lifecycleId_mutant_scopeOnCompleted).
- When an ExecutionCompleted event is emitted, and whether every run emits one, is EVT-003; this block says only which ID it carries. Rust and Python are out of scope: their lifecycle events have no ID field (executor_core/executor.rs 84-88 and 281-286, kept off so as not to change the session archive format, EVT-025). That the IDs of two executors differ is EVT_002_executionId; evt002_started_ids_apart shows that the two blocks together keep the ExecutionStarted events of two executors apart.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_lifecycleId_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✓ The reference lifecycle IDs meet the block: both events of every run are built from the executor's own ID.
  <pre>EVT_002_lifecycleId refLifecycleIds</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_lifecycleId_mutant_freshDraw` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✗ Drawing a fresh ID for the `ExecutionStarted` event violates the block (line 1): the first executor has the ID "0" and its `ExecutionStarted` carries "1". Its executor IDs "0", "2", "4" … are still apart, so it meets `EVT_002_executionId`, and its `ExecutionCompleted` events carry the right ID.
  <pre>evt002_idsApartLine2 evt002_freshDraw ∧ ¬EVT_002_lifecycleId evt002_freshDraw</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_lifecycleId_mutant_scopeOnCompleted` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✗ Putting the ν execution scope on the `ExecutionCompleted` event violates the block (line 2): the first executor has the ID "0" and its `ExecutionCompleted` carries "scope-0". Its `ExecutionStarted` events carry the right ID.
  <pre>evt002_lifeLine1 evt002_scopeOnCompleted ∧ ¬EVT_002_lifecycleId evt002_scopeOnCompleted</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_002_lifecycleId_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_002): ✓ The block is exercised by the reference: the second executor constructed while the clock reads 5 has the ID "1", and its first and second runs both announce and complete with "1".
  <pre>refLifecycleIds.exec 1 5 = "1" ∧<br>  refLifecycleIds.onStarted 1 5 0 = "1" ∧<br>    refLifecycleIds.onCompleted 1 5 0 = "1" ∧<br>      refLifecycleIds.onStarted 1 5 1 = "1" ∧ refLifecycleIds.onCompleted 1 5 1 = "1"</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.joint_events_exec_sketch` (Libpetri.Spec.ConsistencyEvents): ✓ The executor part of the event requirements: the one executor every execution block of wave W5 holds of (with its validator, expiry handling, queue firing and timed step), and an executor with events that steps exactly as it and meets every executor event block, with the action log and the `awaitTermination` answer it offers; over string place names the same executor also meets EVT-014; beside them, the execution IDs, the lifecycle IDs and the run duration. For example, a run that fires one transition and quiesces emits `ExecutionStarted` first and `ExecutionCompleted` last, once each, every token a start takes is reported by one `TokenRemoved` event of its place, and with places declared as `b`, `c`, `a` the marking at the start is reported as `a` then `b`.
  <pre>∀ {N T : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N],<br>  (∃ V E X Q R W A Aw, ExecSpec V E X Q R ∧ W.erase = E ∧ EventsSpec W A Aw) ∧<br>    (∃ V E X Q R W A Aw,<br>        ExecSpec V E X Q R ∧ W.erase = E ∧ EventsSpec W A Aw ∧ EVT_014 W) ∧<br>      (∃ ids, EVT_002_executionId ids) ∧<br>        (∃ L, EVT_002_lifecycleId L) ∧ ∃ d, EVT_003_duration d</pre>

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-EVT_003"></a>
## EVT-003: ExecutionCompleted Event

`Libpetri.Spec.EVT_003` · Kind **B** · Scope all executors (event store enabled) · Source **verbatim** (spec/08-events-observability.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 6ab2e9a77baa85da ai** · Statement hash `6ab2e9a77baa85da`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *When* the executor finishes a run ([EXEC-041]), it *shall* emit exactly one ExecutionCompleted event, whatever the termination reason.<br><br>The executor *shall* emit ExecutionCompleted events only when it finishes a run.<br><br>*If* the executor has emitted the ExecutionCompleted event of a run, *then* it *shall not* emit another event of that run other than a log message ([EVT-013]) or an ActionTimedOut event ([EVT-010]).<br><br>*When* the executor finishes a run with the termination reason `quiescent` ([EXEC-040]), it *shall* have no firing in flight, so every firing of the run has ended before its ExecutionCompleted event. | 1. For every executor with events E and every configuration C:<br>2. the events a run emits before its first step contain no ExecutionCompleted event, whatever the initial marking, and for every history H a step labelled l from state s to state s' that appends the events evs appends exactly one ExecutionCompleted event if it leaves the loop (s is in a phase of the loop and s' in a finished phase), whatever its label and termination reason, and none otherwise;<br>3. for every initial marking M0, every initial reading r0 and every event trace tr of a run of E from M0 at r0 (the events the run emits before its first step, then the events of each step), no event of tr after an ExecutionCompleted event is an orchestrator event, that is an event other than a log message or an ActionTimedOut event;<br>4. for every history H, a step labelled l from state s to state s' that appends the events evs and leaves the loop with the termination reason quiescent (s is in a phase of the loop and s' in the finished phase done quiescent), whatever its label, happens only from a state with no firing in flight. | <pre>fun {N T} E ↦<br>  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),<br>    ((∀ (M0 : QMarking N T),<br>          ∀ e ∈ E.boot C M0, e.kind ≠ NetEventKind.executionCompleted) ∧<br>        ∀ (H : List (NetEvent N T)) (l : XLbl N T) (evs : List (NetEvent N T)),<br>          on fun s s' ↦ E.step C H s l evs s', shall fun s s' ↦<br>            kindCount NetEventKind.executionCompleted evs =<br>              if (isExecPhase s.phase &amp;&amp; !isExecPhase s'.phase) = true then 1 else 0) ∧<br>      (∀ (M0 : QMarking N T) (r0 : ℕ) (tr : List (NetEvent N T)),<br>          Trace E C M0 r0 tr →<br>            (after fun e ↦ e.kind == NetEventKind.executionCompleted, never fun e ↦<br>                e.isOrch)<br>              tr) ∧<br>        ∀ (H : List (NetEvent N T)) (l : XLbl N T) (evs : List (NetEvent N T)),<br>          on fun s s' ↦<br>            E.step C H s l evs s' ∧<br>              isExecPhase s.phase = true ∧ s'.phase = Phase.done Cause.quiescent,<br>            shall fun s x ↦ s.fl = []</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is an executor with events E : EvExec N T (Reference/Events.lean): the events a run emits before its first step, and a step relation E.step C H s l evs s' saying that the step labelled l leads from s to s' and appends the events evs, given the events H emitted before it. Trace E C M0 r0 tr says that tr is what E emits on some run from the initial state of M0. A trace is a finite prefix of a run, so line 2 holds after every step. A run finishes with a step finish c, whose cause c is the termination reason of EXEC-041 (quiescent, terminal, closed or stopped). Line 1 reads 'finishes' off the states, not off the label: a step finishes the run when it leaves the loop, from a phase of the loop (isExecPhase) to a finished phase, whatever it is labelled, so an executor that leaves its loop without a finish step still owes the event. Line 3 reads the quiescent finish the same way: a step from a phase of the loop into the finished phase done quiescent, whose cause is the termination reason the caller reads (EXEC-041, its first line), whatever it is labelled. The witness is the reference executor with events refEvExec under both emission variants (polJT for Java and TypeScript, polRust for Rust and Python): every finish emits ExecutionCompleted last, after the Java and TypeScript snapshot of the marking, and no other step emits one. refEvExec_erase (Reference/EventsLink.lean) shows that it steps exactly as RefExec, so lines 1 and 2 constrain what is emitted; line 3 constrains when a quiescent finish may happen.
- Line 1 is the first two quoted sentences. An executor that announces the end only of a quiescent run, and emits nothing when a terminal place stops the run, breaks it (EVT_003_mutant_quiescentOnly); so does one that announces the end each time the loop parks to wait for an event, because a reactive net that waits has not finished (EVT_003_mutant_atPark); so does one that can leave its loop at the end of a firing pass without a finish step and so emits nothing (EVT_003_mutant_leavesWithoutFinish), the shape of TypeScript's executeLoop, which emits ExecutionCompleted after its while loop with no try/finally (typescript/src/runtime/bitmap-net-executor.ts 523-590), if a cycle threw. The reference leaves its loop only by a finish (EXEC-041, its last line), so on it the two readings agree (evt003_ref_leaves). The boot half of line 1 (no ExecutionCompleted before the first step) has no mutant of its own: an executor that announces the end at the boot breaks line 2 as well as soon as a later step emits an orchestrator event (EVT_003_mutant_bootCompleted keeps line 3 and the step half of line 1).
- Line 2 is the third quoted sentence. 'Another event of that run' reads the trace of one run: a second run of the same executor is a run of its own, with its own ExecutionStarted (EVT-002). An executor that reports a late completion of an abandoned firing after the end breaks it (EVT_003_mutant_lateCompletion). Log messages and ActionTimedOut events are left out on purpose (rulings D74 (a) and R7 (a) of the events design): Java and TypeScript emit ActionTimedOut from the action's own timer, off the orchestrator loop (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/BitmapNetExecutor.java 1751, PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 2378; typescript/src/runtime/bitmap-net-executor.ts 1142-1154), with no check that the run is still going, so a firing a terminal stop abandoned can time out after ExecutionCompleted (EVT_003_allows_inFlightAtTerminal); an abandoned action can still log. The reference emits ActionTimedOut after the end under polJT for the same reason. Whether ActionTimedOut after the end is itself allowed is EVT-010's (ruling D65).
- Line 3 is the fourth quoted sentence: only a quiescent finish has nothing in flight (ruling D74 (a)). An executor that finishes quiescent while firings are still in flight breaks it (EVT_003_mutant_earlyQuiescent); so does one that enters done quiescent with firings in flight under a step that is not labelled a finish (EVT_003_mutant_relabelQuiescent), the shape of an executor that computes the termination reason from the state after its loop exits rather than from the step that ended it, as TypeScript does (typescript/src/runtime/bitmap-net-executor.ts 571-573 sets quiescent whenever the run is neither terminal nor closed). Line 3 does not lean on EXEC-041's last line (a step that leaves the loop is a finish): reading it off the phases, it holds on its own. On the reference the two readings agree: it leaves the loop only by a finish (evt003_ref_leaves), a finish c enters done c (EXEC-041, its first line), and a quiescent finish needs Rest (evt003_line3_emitExec). The other termination reasons do not wait: a terminal stop abandons the firings in flight (EXEC-042) and an immediate termination does too (ENV-015), and the reference emits ExecutionCompleted at such a stop with a firing in flight (EVT_003_allows_inFlightAtTerminal), so a reading that waits for every transition to complete before the event would forbid the run EXEC-042 asks for. Line 3 follows from EXEC-041's line on the quiescent reason (Rest, ruling D13 (a)); here it is the event's reading: the ExecutionCompleted of a quiescent run comes after the end of every firing. AC2 (at a quiescent finish no firing is in flight; a terminal stop or an immediate termination may leave firings in flight) is line 3, EVT_003_allows_inFlightAtTerminal and EVT_003_allows_inFlightAtStop (an immediate termination finishes the run stopped with a firing still in flight, and its finish emits one ExecutionCompleted).
- AC1 (emitted exactly once per run that finishes, whatever the termination reason, and followed by no event of the run other than a log message or an ActionTimedOut) is lines 1 and 2 together: in every trace there is at most one ExecutionCompleted (evt003_atMostOnce, since it is itself an orchestrator event), and a run that finishes has exactly one (evt003_exactlyOnce). A run that has not finished has none: a loop that the timeout policy of a caller's run budget leaves running has not finished (EXEC-041's run budget sentence), so TypeScript, whose run() rejects under the default abandon policy while the loop goes on (typescript/src/runtime/bitmap-net-executor.ts 493-518), emits the event when the loop finishes, not when the caller's run ends.
- The event carries no termination reason, and a consumer reads the reason as EXEC-041 says (the return value, the queryable reason, or a raised error). The ExecutionCompleted event is the end-of-run marker every runtime emits for every reason, not the completion signal EXEC-041 forbids to share between a quiesced and a truncated run: no line here reads the event as proof that the net quiesced. Interrupted (Java's cancellation observed in the wait) is not a cause of the model; Java emits ExecutionCompleted on that path too, after a WARN log message (BitmapNetExecutor.java 1080-1096), which meets line 2. All runtimes emit the event once, at the end of the loop: Java in the finally block of the run loop (BitmapNetExecutor.java 1062-1096, PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 1923-1924), TypeScript after the loop (bitmap-net-executor.ts 570-588, precompiled-net-executor.ts 635-640), Rust at the end of run_sync and of the asynchronous run (rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor_core/executor.rs 476-482 and 1234-1240), which Python runs on.
- The payload is not modelled in this block (ruling D38 (a)): the timestamp (the epoch clock is the CORE-011 slice) and the net name are listed in the markdown without a shall sentence; the execution ID on the event is EVT-002's third block, EVT_002_lifecycleId; the total duration is this requirement's second block, EVT_003_duration. Rust and Python events carry neither ID nor duration (rust/libpetri-event/src/net_event.rs ExecutionCompleted).
- Assumptions shared by the executor event blocks: the event store is enabled and its append does not fail (EVT-020; Java swallows a failing append of ExecutionCompleted, BitmapNetExecutor.java 1097-1098); an event is a value (EVT-001); transition names are distinct (ruling D10). The events of one step are contiguous in the model, since a step appends its events at once. Java appends ActionTimedOut events and the log messages it captures from actions from other threads than the orchestrator (the timeout callback BitmapNetExecutor.fireTransition hands java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/ExecutorSupport.java withActionTimeout, which appends through emitEvent from the timer thread; LogCaptureScope.java wrapRunnable and wrapCallable), so in a Java store such an event can fall between the events of one step; the lines are read on the store with those events left out, as the reading at the top of spec/08-events-observability.md says. TypeScript and Rust append every event from the orchestrator.
- The test derivation (run a net to quiescence, verify the last event is ExecutionCompleted, emitted once) is EVT_003_nonvacuous: a run that fires one transition and quiesces ends with ExecutionCompleted, emitted once. 'Last' holds of a quiescent run; after a terminal stop an ActionTimedOut of an abandoned firing may follow (EVT_003_allows_inFlightAtTerminal). The duration check of the test derivation is the second block's.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-EVT_003_duration"></a>
## EVT-003: ExecutionCompleted Event (total duration)

`Libpetri.Spec.EVT_003_duration` · Kind **F** · Scope Java and TypeScript executors (the ExecutionCompleted event of Rust and Python carries no duration) · Source **verbatim** (spec/08-events-observability.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 ad794fa3f6d75029 ai** · Statement hash `ad794fa3f6d75029`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *Where* the ExecutionCompleted event carries a total duration (Java and TypeScript), the total duration *shall* be at least the time the run took on the executor's firing clock ([TIME-015]), from the reading at its ExecutionStarted event to the reading at its ExecutionCompleted event. | 1. For every duration assignment dur, where dur b r e is the total duration the ExecutionCompleted event of a run carries when the executor's firing clock read b when the executor was built, r when the run emitted its ExecutionStarted event and e when it emits its ExecutionCompleted event: for all readings with b ≤ r ≤ e, the duration is at least e - r. | <pre>fun dur ↦ ∀ (b r e : ℕ), b ≤ r → r ≤ e → e - r ≤ dur b r e</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- This is the second block of EVT-003 and the Java and TypeScript companion of ruling D38 (a), which states durations as bounds: the event model of the first block (NetEvent in Spec/GlossaryEvents.lean) carries no duration and the executor state no start reading, so this block states the duration over what a host observes, three readings of the executor's firing clock and the duration on the event, and needs no new field. The firing clock is the executor's injected clock of TIME-015 (the system's monotonic clock by default), so its readings never decrease: b ≤ r ≤ e. The epoch clock that stamps events (CORE-011) is not read.
- Java and TypeScript measure the duration from the construction of the executor, not from the start of the run: Java as clockNanos() - startNanos with startNanos taken in the constructor (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/BitmapNetExecutor.java 354 and 2551, PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 355 and 2941-2942), TypeScript as nowMs() - startMs with startMs taken in the constructor (typescript/src/runtime/bitmap-net-executor.ts 360 and 587, precompiled-net-executor.ts 377 and 639). The witness refDurOf is that difference, e - b. It meets the line because b ≤ r. For the first run of a fresh executor it is the run's own time plus the time between construction and run(); for a later run of the same executor it also counts the earlier runs and the time between them. The line is a bound, so both are allowed (EVT_003_duration_nonvacuous).
- The line is the quoted sentence and AC3 (where the event carries a total duration, it is at least the time the run took on the executor's firing clock). An executor that leaves the duration at zero breaks it on every run during which the clock advances (EVT_003_duration_forbids_zero). The test derivation checks the bound with a firing clock that advances during the run; under an injected clock that does not move, the duration may be 0 and still meet the line.
- The model is a restriction: the duration is a function of the three readings only, so a duration that depends on anything else (the number of firings, a second clock) cannot be written as an assignment. Rust and Python are out of scope: their ExecutionCompleted event has no duration field (rust/libpetri-event/src/net_event.rs ExecutionCompleted carries the net name and timestamp only). When the event is emitted is the first block's; the shared assumptions of the executor event blocks (store enabled, events are values) apply.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_003_duration_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_003): ✓ The reference total duration meets the block: measured from the construction of the executor, it is never less than the time since the run started.
  <pre>EVT_003_duration refDurOf</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_003_duration_forbids_zero` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_003): ✗ Leaving the duration at zero violates the block: a run from reading 0 to reading 5 reports 0, less than the 5 it took.
  <pre>¬EVT_003_duration evt003_durZero</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_003_duration_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_003): ✓ The block is exercised by the reference: an executor built at reading 0 whose first run goes from 0 to 5 reports 5; its second run, from 10 to 15, reports 15, more than its own 5, which the bound allows.
  <pre>refDurOf 0 0 5 = 5 ∧ refDurOf 0 10 15 = 15 ∧ 15 - 10 ≤ refDurOf 0 10 15</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.joint_events_exec_sketch` (Libpetri.Spec.ConsistencyEvents): ✓ The executor part of the event requirements: the one executor every execution block of wave W5 holds of (with its validator, expiry handling, queue firing and timed step), and an executor with events that steps exactly as it and meets every executor event block, with the action log and the `awaitTermination` answer it offers; over string place names the same executor also meets EVT-014; beside them, the execution IDs, the lifecycle IDs and the run duration. For example, a run that fires one transition and quiesces emits `ExecutionStarted` first and `ExecutionCompleted` last, once each, every token a start takes is reported by one `TokenRemoved` event of its place, and with places declared as `b`, `c`, `a` the marking at the start is reported as `a` then `b`.
  <pre>∀ {N T : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N],<br>  (∃ V E X Q R W A Aw, ExecSpec V E X Q R ∧ W.erase = E ∧ EventsSpec W A Aw) ∧<br>    (∃ V E X Q R W A Aw,<br>        ExecSpec V E X Q R ∧ W.erase = E ∧ EventsSpec W A Aw ∧ EVT_014 W) ∧<br>      (∃ ids, EVT_002_executionId ids) ∧<br>        (∃ L, EVT_002_lifecycleId L) ∧ ∃ d, EVT_003_duration d</pre>

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-EVT_004"></a>
## EVT-004: TransitionEnabled Event

`Libpetri.Spec.EVT_004` · Kind **B** · Scope all executors (event store enabled) · Source **verbatim** (spec/08-events-observability.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 df28d0366afcb820 ai** · Statement hash `df28d0366afcb820`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled in this requirement means armed: a transition that is armed again after its own firing, after the enablement recheck of a firing pass disarmed it, or after a reap and a later write of one of its arc places is announced again, even when the marking kept it enabled.<br><br>A transition whose clock restarts while it stays armed is announced with `TransitionClockRestarted` instead ([EVT-005]).<br><br>*When* a transition is armed after an enablement update and was not armed before it, the executor *shall* emit, at that update, exactly one TransitionEnabled event naming the transition.<br><br>The executor *shall* emit a TransitionEnabled event naming a transition only at an enablement update before which the transition was not armed and after which it is armed. | 1. For every executor with events E and every configuration C:<br>2. when the transition names of C's net are pairwise distinct, for every history H, an enablement update from state s to state s' that appends the events evs contains, for every name n, exactly one TransitionEnabled event naming n if n is a transition of the net that is not armed in s and armed in s', and none otherwise;<br>3. the events a run emits before its first step contain no TransitionEnabled event, whatever the initial marking, and for every history H a step whose label is not the enablement update appends no TransitionEnabled event. | <pre>fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] E ↦<br>  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),<br>    (NamesDistinct C.X →<br>        ∀ (H evs : List (NetEvent N T)) (n : String),<br>          on fun s s' ↦ E.step C H s XLbl.update evs s', shall fun s s' ↦<br>            namedCount NetEventKind.transitionEnabled n evs =<br>              if<br>                  n ∈ List.map (fun x ↦ x.core.name) C.X.net.transitions ∧<br>                    isArmedS (s.st n) = false ∧ isArmedS (s'.st n) = true then<br>                1<br>              else 0) ∧<br>      (∀ (M0 : QMarking N T),<br>          ∀ e ∈ E.boot C M0, e.kind ≠ NetEventKind.transitionEnabled) ∧<br>        ∀ (H : List (NetEvent N T)) (l : XLbl N T) (evs : List (NetEvent N T)),<br>          l ≠ XLbl.update →<br>            on fun s s' ↦ E.step C H s l evs s', shall fun x x_1 ↦<br>              ∀ e ∈ evs, e.kind ≠ NetEventKind.transitionEnabled</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is an executor with events E : EvExec N T (Reference/Events.lean): the events a run emits before its first step, and a step relation E.step C H s l evs s' saying that the step labelled l leads from s to s' and appends the events evs, given the events H emitted before it. The witness is the reference executor with events refEvExec, the reference executor RefExec with its emission refEmitW, under both emission variants (polJT for Java and TypeScript, polRust for Rust and Python). refEvExec_erase (Reference/EventsLink.lean) shows that it steps exactly as RefExec, so the block constrains what is emitted and nothing else. Both lines hold for every history H. The block reads an event only through its kind and the transition name it carries (namedCount), which every runtime's TransitionEnabled carries; the timestamp is not modelled (the epoch clock is the CORE-011 slice), so there is no payload companion.
- Enabled is read as Armed (rulings D5 and D39, clash evt-a#1): armed is the executor's clock status (isArmedS of the status, GlossaryExec Status.armed), set only by the enablement update. The body sentence and both acceptance criteria say armed. Read as the marking-level Enabled, the requirement would contradict every runtime, which announce a transition again after its own firing and after a reaped transition is re-armed although the marking never disabled it (Rust bitmap_backend.rs post_fire 883-890 and update_enablement 615-619, emitted at executor_core/executor.rs 579-585; Java BitmapNetExecutor.java 1313-1319; TypeScript bitmap-net-executor.ts 748-756). A transition whose clock restart is pending ([TIME-012], EVT-005) is still armed before the update (it keeps its old stamp until then), so it gets no TransitionEnabled: the second line of each block and the per-update image of TIME-012 AC6 are in EVT_005.lean.
- Armed is read from the executor's own state, and the block says nothing about what a start, a recheck or an update does to that state: TIME_012_cycle (a start leaves the started transition off, the recheck's lose turns a transition off, the update stamps a pending transition afresh and clears its flag) and TIME_010_cycle do, on the same executor through W.erase = E in the joint theorem of the event blocks. So EVT-004 alone allows an executor whose start leaves the started transition armed with its old stamp; it reports nothing when r is armed again after its own firing in the worked example, and TIME_012_cycle line 2 rejects its steps (EVT_004_allows_startKeepsArmed). That executor is the slip of Rust post_fire without its enabled_flags clear (bitmap_backend.rs 883-890) or of Java's fire path without clearEnabledBit; no runtime ships it.
- Line 1 is the third and fourth quoted sentences at the update: exactly one event for a transition that is armed after the update and was not armed before it (the markdown says exactly one), none for one that stays armed, none for one the update leaves unarmed. AC1 (emitted each time a transition that was not armed before an enablement update is armed after it) is the first case, AC2 (not emitted if the transition was already armed, also when its clock restarts) the second. The second quoted sentence is line 1 for a restarted transition, which is armed before the update and so gets no TransitionEnabled; that it gets one TransitionClockRestarted is EVT_005 line 1, and evt005_one_of (EVT_005.lean) shows that the two blocks together report each such update of a transition with exactly one of the two events. An executor that does not announce a transition that has already started in the run when it is armed again breaks line 1 (EVT_004_mutant_silentSelf, the event image of announcing on the marking-level edge), so does one that also announces a restarted transition (EVT_004_forbids_bothEvents) and one that announces every armed transition at every update (EVT_004_forbids_everyUpdate). The line counts per name, so it needs the names of the net pairwise distinct (ruling D10; the builders reject a duplicate name; the markdown states the assumption, as TIME-010 does for the timing requirements); the reference emits one event per declared transition.
- Line 2 is the fourth quoted sentence away from the update: no TransitionEnabled at the boot of a run (the first update arms what the initial marking enables) and none at any other step. An executor that announces the transitions the initial marking enables when it boots breaks it (EVT_004_mutant_bootEnabled), and so does one that announces a transition as soon as a completion's deposit enables it in the marking, before an update arms it (EVT_004_mutant_atCommit). Every runtime emits TransitionEnabled at one place only, its enablement update (Rust executor_core/executor.rs 579-585, Java BitmapNetExecutor.java 1318 and PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 2044, TypeScript bitmap-net-executor.ts 753 and precompiled-net-executor.ts 803), which Python runs on.
- Not fixed here: the order of the TransitionEnabled and TransitionClockRestarted events inside one update (Rust emits every TransitionEnabled first, executor_core/executor.rs 579-592; Java and TypeScript emit each event as they scan, so no line orders them), and which transitions an update may arm while a firing of them is in flight (ruling D8: Java and TypeScript skip a transition in flight, BitmapNetExecutor.java 1309 and bitmap-net-executor.ts 743; Rust arms it again; both are runs of RefExec, Cfg.reentrant, and the line is an arming edge that holds for both). That every TransitionStarted of a transition follows a TransitionEnabled or TransitionClockRestarted of it since its previous start is a trace corollary not stated here. Assumptions shared by the executor event blocks: the event store is enabled (EVT-020; Rust skips the events when it is not, executor_core/executor.rs 593-596) and its append does not fail; an event is a value (EVT-001).
- The test derivation (add a token enabling a transition, verify TransitionEnabled for it) is EVT_004_nonvacuous: in the worked example the second update reports r, which its own start disarmed, and not T, which stays armed; the boot reports no TransitionEnabled although the initial marking enables both transitions; and with two tokens in place 0 the second update reports nothing for T, which keeps its stamp.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_004_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_004): ✓ The reference executor with the Java and TypeScript emission meets EVT-004: each update reports, once, every transition it arms that was not armed before it, and nothing else reports `TransitionEnabled`.

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.EVT_004_rust` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.EVT_004): ✓ The reference executor with the Rust and Python emission meets EVT-004 too: the block is a line for every executor.

What a start does to that status is [TIME-012]'s: its companion line on the cycle (a start leaves the started transition off) rejects the steps of this executor, so only the two requirements together, on the same executor, rule it out.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-EVT_005"></a>
## EVT-005: TransitionClockRestarted Event

`Libpetri.Spec.EVT_005` · Kind **B** · Scope all executors (event store enabled) · Source **verbatim** (spec/08-events-observability.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 01f4e8f08fa9c62d ai** · Statement hash `01f4e8f08fa9c62d`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| A transition's clock restart is pending when it is armed, a start of another transition since the last enablement update left it not enabled in that start's intermediate marking ([TIME-012]), and neither the enablement recheck of a firing pass nor a start of its own has disarmed it since.<br><br>An enablement update restarts the clock of a transition when it leaves the transition armed with the update's clock reading as its stamp and its clock restart no longer pending.<br><br>*When* an enablement update restarts the clock of a transition whose clock restart was pending before the update, the executor *shall* emit, at that update, exactly one TransitionClockRestarted event naming the transition.<br><br>The executor *shall* emit a TransitionClockRestarted event naming a transition only at an enablement update before which the transition's clock restart was pending and that restarts the transition's clock. | 1. For every executor with events E and every configuration C:<br>2. when the transition names of C's net are pairwise distinct, for every history H, an enablement update from state s to state s' that appends the events evs contains, for every name n, exactly one TransitionClockRestarted event naming n if n is a transition of the net whose clock restart is pending in s and whose status in s' is armed at the cycle reading of s' with no restart pending, and none otherwise;<br>3. the events a run emits before its first step contain no TransitionClockRestarted event, whatever the initial marking, and for every history H a step whose label is not the enablement update appends no TransitionClockRestarted event. | <pre>fun {N T} [DecidableEq N] E ↦<br>  ∀ (C : Cfg N T),<br>    (NamesDistinct C.X →<br>        ∀ (H evs : List (NetEvent N T)) (n : String),<br>          on fun s s' ↦ E.step C H s XLbl.update evs s', shall fun s s' ↦<br>            namedCount NetEventKind.transitionClockRestarted n evs =<br>              if<br>                  n ∈ List.map (fun x ↦ x.core.name) C.X.net.transitions ∧<br>                    pendingS (s.st n) = true ∧ s'.st n = Status.armed s'.cyc false then<br>                1<br>              else 0) ∧<br>      (∀ (M0 : QMarking N T),<br>          ∀ e ∈ E.boot C M0, e.kind ≠ NetEventKind.transitionClockRestarted) ∧<br>        ∀ (H : List (NetEvent N T)) (l : XLbl N T) (evs : List (NetEvent N T)),<br>          l ≠ XLbl.update →<br>            on fun s s' ↦ E.step C H s l evs s', shall fun x x_1 ↦<br>              ∀ e ∈ evs, e.kind ≠ NetEventKind.transitionClockRestarted</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is an executor with events E : EvExec N T (Reference/Events.lean), as in EVT_004: the boot events of a run and a step relation E.step C H s l evs s' with the history H of the events emitted before the step. The witness is refEvExec, RefExec with its emission refEmitW, under both emission variants (polJT for Java and TypeScript, polRust for Rust and Python); refEvExec_erase (Reference/EventsLink.lean) shows that it steps exactly as RefExec. Both lines hold for every history H. The block reads an event only through its kind and the transition name it carries (namedCount, EVT_004.lean); the timestamp is not modelled, so there is no payload companion.
- Restart pending is the executor status Status.armed k true (pendingS, the proposed glossary term Restart pending of Reference/Events.lean; rulings D5, D7 and D39, clashes evt-a#2 and evt-a#15): afterStart sets it on every other armed transition the start's live intermediate marking disables (TIME-012); a start of the transition itself turns it off, the enablement recheck of the pass turns it off (lose), and the next update clears it, re-stamping the transition if it finds it enabled and turning it off otherwise. This is the observed gap of the body: the runtimes keep the enabled flag of such a transition and set a restart bit (Rust bitmap_backend.rs flag_clock_restarts 425-439 and update_enablement 624-639; Java BitmapNetExecutor.java 1324-1336; TypeScript bitmap-net-executor.ts 760-780), and clear the enabled flag on a failed recheck while the bit is ignored, so the next update reports TransitionEnabled (Rust executor_core/executor.rs 423-435, bitmap_backend.rs disable 892-898). Java does not flag a transition in flight (BitmapNetExecutor.java 1872) and Rust does; in RefExec a transition in flight is off and never flagged, so both are runs of it (ruling D8). A restart of the clock is the status the update leaves: armed at the update's reading s'.cyc with the flag cleared (Status.armed s'.cyc false), which is what TIME_012_cycle line 3 says an update does to a pending transition it finds enabled; at a reference update a pending transition is armed after it exactly when this holds (updW_pending_iff). Pending is read from the executor's own state, and when a start sets it is TIME_012_cycle line 1's, on the same executor through W.erase = E in the joint theorem of the event blocks. So EVT-005 alone allows an executor whose start never flags a restart: in the worked example it reports neither event for T, which keeps its old stamp, and TIME_012_cycle line 1 rejects its steps (EVT_005_allows_neverFlags).
- Line 1 is the second, third and fourth quoted sentences at the update: exactly one event for a transition whose clock restart was pending and whose clock the update restarts (the markdown says exactly one), none for any other name, so none on initial enablement and none on re-enablement after an observed disablement (AC2: both are TransitionEnabled, EVT_004 line 1), and none for a transition that keeps its clock (TIME-012 AC4, EVT_005_time012_ac4). AC1 (emitted only when the transition stays armed but its clock restarts) is the line read from left to right. An executor that does not report a restart breaks it (EVT_005_mutant_silentRestart), and so does one that reports the fired transition, armed again after its own firing, as restarted (EVT_005_forbids_restartOnOwnFiring). Because the line asks for the fresh stamp and the cleared flag, it also rejects an update that reports the restart but keeps the old stamp (EVT_005_mutant_keepStamp: the update rule before 6.0.0 with the 6.0.0 event, or the restart branch without its stamp assignment, Rust bitmap_backend.rs 629, Java BitmapNetExecutor.java 1327, TypeScript bitmap-net-executor.ts 768) and one that leaves the restart flag set and so reports the restart again at a later update with no start in between (EVT_005_mutant_keepFlag: the scan without its trailing clear, Rust bitmap_backend.rs 636-639, Java BitmapNetExecutor.java 1334-1337, TypeScript bitmap-net-executor.ts 778-781). The line counts per name, so it needs the names of the net pairwise distinct (ruling D10; the markdown states the assumption, as in EVT-004).
- Line 2 is the fourth quoted sentence away from the update: no TransitionClockRestarted at the boot of a run or at any step but the update. An executor that reports the restart already at the start that takes the clock breaks it (EVT_005_mutant_eagerRestart), and so does one that reports a restart for the transitions the initial marking enables when the run boots (EVT_005_mutant_bootRestarted). Every runtime emits TransitionClockRestarted at its enablement update only (Rust executor_core/executor.rs 587-592, Java BitmapNetExecutor.java 1328 and PrecompiledNetExecutor.java 2054, TypeScript bitmap-net-executor.ts 770 and precompiled-net-executor.ts 820).
- Not fixed here: the order of the events inside one update (Rust reports every TransitionEnabled before every TransitionClockRestarted, executor_core/executor.rs 579-592; Java and TypeScript report each as they scan). That one update never reports both events for one name, and that every update that arms a transition afresh or restarts its pending clock reports exactly one of the two, follow from this block and EVT_004 together (evt005_one_of, cited for TIME-012 AC6 in its per-update form; the run-level count, each restart announced exactly once by a later update, is not stated). Assumptions shared by the executor event blocks: the event store is enabled (EVT-020) and its append does not fail; an event is a value (EVT-001).
- The test derivation is EVT_005_nonvacuous: in EVT-004's worked example the update after the refresh reports TransitionClockRestarted once for T, whose clock restart is pending, and none for r, armed again after its own start; and the boot reports none. Its second sentence (an executor that re-evaluates between the consumption and the deposit reports TransitionEnabled instead) is EVT_005_time012_ac6: with r's action asynchronous, the update between its start and its deposit turns T off, and the update after the deposit reports TransitionEnabled for T. As clash evt-a#2 notes, T must not be ready in the pass (the derivation says armed but not yet ready): a ready T that comes after the consuming transition fails the enablement recheck of the pass, loses its clock there and is reported with TransitionEnabled, which is the last clause of the derivation (EVT_005_nonvacuous_readyRecheck).
