**Assumptions**

- Ruling D54 (a) (clash mod-c#2, R-MC6): the canonical member is the first declared member of a set and keeps its own name; the set's name is used in diagnostics only, as every runtime does (rust/libpetri-core/src/fusion.rs:17-21, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/core/FusionSet.java:24-27, typescript/src/core/fusion-set.ts:23-27). That fixed choice is what makes the fused structure a function of the declaration (substSpec_unique). One-member sets and the declaration check (empty set, token types) are MOD-060's; a one-member set fuses nothing (refFuse_short). MOD-060 states the same choice (item 1, item 2 and AC4); step 1 of MOD-061 does not cite it.
- Model scope. A fusion function works on what the builder holds after every compose call (FuseNet: places, CDef definitions in declaration order per ruling D32 (a), terminal places), as Rust build_with_fusion (rust/libpetri-core/src/petri_net.rs:855-1002), Java buildWithFusion (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/core/PetriNet.java:1118-1197) and TypeScript buildWithFusion (typescript/src/core/petri-net.ts:793-879) do; Python rides on Rust. FuseNet has no field for fusion sets, so the sentence 'the built net keeps no record of the fusion sets' holds by construction. That fusion runs after every compose call and before CORE-040 returns the net (item 'Fusion MUST be applied after all compose(...) calls' and AC4's 'composing then fusing is observationally equivalent to a hand-written net'), that the retired-port check of MOD-027 and the terminal check of EXEC-042 run on the fused net, and that removed members lose their subnet membership entry (MOD-026) are ComposeBuild's finish (composition wave W8, MOD-023, MOD-026, MOD-027). Line 6 says that fusion itself succeeds; those later checks may still fail build().
- Line 1 compares definitions as TransDef, not as CDef: the declared-to-actual correspondence a rewrite records is MOD-031's (Rust keeps none when every entry is the identity, the MAY of MOD-031). The list equality fixes order and number: a result that drops or reorders a transition breaks it. 'An input arc on a member that is not the first declared member of its set' is an input arc on a place σ moves (fuseTouches): the merge runs on exactly those transitions (Rust apply_fusion inputs_touched, rust/libpetri-core/src/rewriter.rs:536-539; Java and TypeScript applyFusion), and then over all its input arcs; a transition whose input arcs are all on places σ fixes, two of them on the first member of a set for example, is not merged and keeps the duplicate, which Build rejects (CORE-030). Read, inhibitor and reset arcs that land on one place are kept as they are in every runtime (rust/libpetri-core/src/rewriter.rs:202-225, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/core/internal/SubnetRewriter.java:239-241, typescript/src/core/internal/subnet-rewriter.ts:223-231), unlike a channel merge (MOD-021 rule (a)).
- Every rewritten transition passes through the transition builder again (line 2; IO-011, IO-012, EXEC-012 and CORE-030 name fusion as a construction path). The sentence that a rewrite the builder rejects fails fusion is mod061_buildFails, a consequence of lines 1 and 2, and the sentence that an off-table pair fails fusion is mod061_offTable, a consequence of line 1. The message of a builder rejection is owned by CORE-030, IO-011, IO-012 and EXEC-012 and is not stated here (skeptic correction S6 of the composition design: the block holds for every Build).
- Line 3 and line 4 compare places and terminal places as sets: the order of places is not normative (ruling D32), Java collects places in a HashSet, and terminals are deduplicated in declaration order by every runtime. Under line 3 a canonical member that is neither declared, nor named by an arc, nor terminal is not a place of the result, as in every runtime (a member is never checked to be a builder place). Line 4 is the sentence of ruling D20 (R-MC8 (a)) that a terminal on a removed member names the canonical member (petri_net.rs:982-992, PetriNet.java:1185-1191, petri-net.ts:864-873).
- A fusion set may list its first member again later (members [a, b, a]). Every runtime skips a later member equal to the canonical member when it builds the fusion map and the removed names (rust/libpetri-core/src/petri_net.rs:907-914, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/core/PetriNet.java:1141-1147, typescript/src/core/petri-net.ts:817-825), so the declared place a remains, as lines 1 and 3 say with the spec's 'the canonical member remains' (step 3): σ fixes a, and the reference keeps a (mod061_dupCanonical_kept).
- Line 5 is the MUST 'the final flat net MUST be independent of that order' and AC6, read as the markdown asks: 'observationally identical', AC6's 'identical place set, transition set, arc topology'. A rejection keeps its message; a success keeps its transitions in order and its places and terminal places as sets, so the order in which the built net lists places is free, as in lines 3 and 4 (mod061_setOrder_meets: a fusion that lists the first members of the sets first, in declaration order, meets MOD-061). The application order inside build() cannot be observed through F; independence from the declaration order covers it, and AC6 is reworded to 'declared in opposite orders'. AC6's 'identical executor behavior' follows, since equal nets run alike. Without disjointness nothing is claimed: overlapping sets are rejected (line 7), and the substitution would not exist (substSpec_overlap).
- Line 7 is the overlap sentence, raised from SHOULD to MUST under ruling D20 (R-MC8 (a)), since every runtime rejects (petri_net.rs:878-895, PetriNet.java:1122-1134, petri-net.ts:797-811) with this message. 'Different' is structural: the two sets differ in name or in members. Declaring the same set (same name, same members) twice is implementation-defined and not covered: Rust rejects it by list position, Java and TypeScript compare set objects with != and fuse one object declared twice once (two separately built equal sets count as different there, which line 7 neither requires nor forbids). Two sets with the same members and different names are different and rejected. Which shared place and which pair the message names when several sets or places overlap is not fixed: the runtimes walk the sets in declaration order and report the first member an earlier set lists, Rust and Java with the first earlier set listing it, TypeScript with the latest; line 7 claims only some shared place and some pair that lists it, earlier set first. With exactly two sets sharing exactly one place the message is determined (mod061_twoSets_msg, a consequence of line 7, and the sentence that states it).
- Lines 8 and 9 state the message of a first offender only (skeptic correction S3): with an earlier transition that fails Build, that failure is reported. The collision is the first off-table pair met while merging left to right, its earlier side the merge of the arcs before it on that place (insertInE; Rust merge_input_arcs, Java mergeInputArcs, TypeScript normalizeInputArcs): one(), one(), then atLeast(1) on one place reports exactly(2) and atLeast(1). Line 8 is a pair on a member of a set (after the substitution, its first member); line 9 is a pair on a place no set lists, for example a duplicate input arc on an unfused place of a transition that also has a moved arc, where every runtime puts the place's own name in the seam (rewriter.rs:559-564, PetriNet.java:1155-1160, petri-net.ts:833-836; a pair on a member lies on the first member after the substitution, the key Rust and Java look up). MOD-021 binds the method spelling of atLeast to the host language, which Rust and Python spell at_least(n) in the cardinality and in the closing hint (rewriter.rs:562-572, :1027-1034); F carries no host language, so lines 8 and 9 accept both spellings and the binding stays MOD-021's.
- AC1 (three leaky-bucket instances share one limiter) is MOD_061_nonvacuous on the reference (every take transition draws from b1/limit). AC2 is reworded under ruling D54 (a) (R-MC7, clash mod-c#1): a token put on a non-canonical member at initial-marking time stays on that undeclared name, retained and inert, which is CORE-072's line; no executor knows a fusion set (rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor_core/executor.rs:502-517). AC3 (non-canonical members are not places of the built net) is mod061_removed, a consequence of lines 1 and 3 for every model. AC4's merge and rejection are lines 1, 8 and 9 and mod061_offTable; its 'after composition' is ComposeBuild's. AC5 (export and verification need no awareness of fusion) is MOD-023's and MOD-050's. AC6 is line 5. AC7 is line 7.
- The test derivation's 'fuse two places each consumed via one() by the same transition; verify the built net consumes 2 from the canonical place' is fuseEx_both_merged on the reference, 'fuse places whose colliding input arcs cannot merge; verify build rejection names the fusion set' is fuseEx_mix_rejected, and 'declare b terminal and fuse {a, b}; verify a is terminal in the built net' is fuseEx_terminal_moved (the first two in MOD_061_nonvacuous).

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.MOD_061_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.MOD_061): ✓ The reference fusion satisfies MOD-061 for every transition-builder check: it rejects two sets that share a place with the runtimes' overlap message, rewrites every definition through the first-member substitution, merging the input arcs of a transition with a moved input arc by the [MOD-021] table, re-runs the check on each, names the fusion set (or, off every set, the place) when a pair does not merge, keeps the places the substitution fixes and does not depend on the order of disjoint sets.
  <pre>∀ {N A : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N] [inst_1 : ToString N]<br>  (Build : Reference.Trans N → Option String), MOD_061 Build (refFuse Build)</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.MOD_061_forbids_noMerge` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.MOD_061): ✗ A fusion that renames without merging violates MOD-061 (line 2): fusing `a` and `b` under a transition that takes `one()` from each leaves two `one()` arcs on `a`, which the reference builder rejects ([CORE-030]), where the table would give a single `exactly(2)` arc.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-NU_001"></a>
## NU-001: Name Identity

`Libpetri.Spec.NU_001` · Kind **F** · Scope the names, the name equality and the name order of each implementation · Source **verbatim** (spec/12-nu-nets.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 61b6b5dab6a7eee4 ai** · Statement hash `61b6b5dab6a7eee4`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| The name constructor *shall* return equal names for equal underlying values and different names for different underlying values.<br><br>Each implementation *shall* order names by one fixed strict total order, the name order: if one name precedes another, the other does not precede it; if a first name precedes a second and the second precedes a third, the first precedes the third; and of two different names, one precedes the other.<br><br>Of two names whose underlying values hold only Basic Multilingual Plane characters, one *shall* precede the other exactly when its value precedes the other's in the lexicographic order of code points. | 1. For all values a and b, the implementation's name equality holds between the name constructed from a and the name constructed from b exactly when a = b.<br>2. For all values a and b, if the name of a precedes the name of b, then the name of b does not precede the name of a (so no name precedes itself).<br>3. For all values a, b and c, if the name of a precedes the name of b and the name of b precedes the name of c, then the name of a precedes the name of c.<br>4. For all different values a and b, the name of a precedes the name of b or the name of b precedes the name of a.<br>5. For all values a and b whose characters all lie below U+10000, the name of a precedes the name of b exactly when a precedes b in the lexicographic order of code points. | <pre>fun I ↦<br>  (∀ (a b : String), I.eq (I.ofValue a) (I.ofValue b) ↔ a = b) ∧<br>    (∀ (a b : String),<br>        I.lt (I.ofValue a) (I.ofValue b) → ¬I.lt (I.ofValue b) (I.ofValue a)) ∧<br>      (∀ (a b c : String),<br>          I.lt (I.ofValue a) (I.ofValue b) →<br>            I.lt (I.ofValue b) (I.ofValue c) → I.lt (I.ofValue a) (I.ofValue c)) ∧<br>        (∀ (a b : String),<br>            a ≠ b → I.lt (I.ofValue a) (I.ofValue b) ∨ I.lt (I.ofValue b) (I.ofValue a)) ∧<br>          ∀ (a b : String),<br>            (∀ c ∈ a.toList, c.toNat &lt; 65536) →<br>              (∀ c ∈ b.toList, c.toNat &lt; 65536) →<br>                (I.lt (I.ofValue a) (I.ofValue b) ↔ a &lt; b)</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is one implementation's NameImpl: the carrier of names, the constructor from the underlying value, the name equality and the name order. A name is what the constructor returns; names minted by the executor (NU-010, NU-011) are constructed from their rendered string, so they are names in this sense. The underlying values are strings of Unicode scalar values (Lean's String), which covers every value Rust and Python accept; Java's rejection of a null value and JavaScript or Java strings holding an unpaired surrogate are outside the model.
- The constructor is a function of the value, so two constructions of one value give one term of the carrier; the name equality is a field, so an implementation whose names compare by object identity, where two constructions of one value are not equal, is a model and breaks the first line (NU_001_mutant_identityEq). Rust derives PartialEq on the string, Java's NameId is a record and TypeScript's NameId is a branded string compared by value: each is the reference equality.
- The fourth line ranges over different underlying values. By the first line these are exactly the pairs of different names, so it is the quote's 'of two different names'; stating it over values keeps it independent of the first line.
- 'Stable' and 'consistent across a single implementation' (AC2) are read as: the name order is one fixed relation of the implementation, a field of NameImpl, so it cannot differ between two comparisons. Whether it is the same relation in two processes of one implementation is not modelled; every runtime fixes it in code (Rust's derived Ord, Java's String.compareTo, TypeScript's string comparison).
- Ruling D31 (a): outside the BMP the order is a parameter. The reference is code-point order (refNameImpl, the order of Rust and of Python, which runs on the Rust runtime); the UTF-16 code-unit order of Java and TypeScript satisfies the block too, agrees with code-point order on BMP names (NU_001_utf16_bmp_agree) and disagrees with it on U+FFFF against U+10000 (NU_001_allows_utf16). The fifth line is what NU-020's 'all languages fire identically' and its note 'byte-identical across implementations for BMP names' rest on for the name half of the tie-break; it rejects a reversed comparator (NU_001_mutant_reversed) and a shortlex order (NU_001_forbids_shortlex). That the oldest-token half of the tie-break agrees across languages is NU-020's and NU-022's, not a line here.
- Ruling D96 (a): the behaviour sentence of NU-001 (a firing reads the names its keys project only through name equality and, for the tie-break of NU-020, the name order) and its event-driven form are the kind B block NU_001_rename in this file, over the ν firing model; they are not lines of this F block. The sentences 'A name (NameId) is an opaque correlation identity, constructed from an underlying string value.' and 'The name order exists solely for that tie-break and carries no domain meaning.' are design text, traced by NU_001_rename.
- 'Identity is a projection of the token payload, not a field on the token' and 'the token model is unchanged' are design text: a match key reads the token value (NU-020), and no model in this development adds a name field to a token. AC3 (adding ν-matching does not change the token type or the on-the-wire shape of token-bearing events) and the test derivation's third check are API and wire shape (kind Q). No test in any language yet runs a net with and without the ν-net APIs and compares its token events, so AC3 has no traced Q evidence; it is recorded here as open, to be closed by a kind Q test beside the EVT-011 and EVT-012 tests.
- AC1 (two names constructed from the same underlying value are equal; from different values, unequal) is the first line. AC2 (a stable total order on names, consistent across a single implementation) is the second, third and fourth lines: a strict total order on names, with stability read as above. AC4 (a one-to-one renaming that keeps the chosen name the chosen name changes no firing) is the renaming line NU_001_rename's.
- The test derivation's first two checks (NameId("a") constructed twice is equal; NameId("a") precedes NameId("b")) follow from the statement for every implementation (NU_001_testDerivation) and are NU_001_nonvacuous on the reference. At runtime the Rust unit tests equality_by_value and total_order_is_lexicographic in rust/libpetri-core/src/name.rs run them.
- Implementations also hash names (Rust's derived Hash, Java's record hashCode, a JavaScript Map key); a hash consistent with the name equality adds no observation, and is not modelled.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): The reference satisfies NU-001: the constructor is the identity, the name equality is string equality, and Lean's `String` order is a strict total order, code-point order everywhere.
  <pre>NU_001 refNameImpl</pre>
- ✓ **allows** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_allows_utf16` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): Ruling D31 (a): NU-001 does not fix the name order outside the BMP. The Java/TypeScript UTF-16 code-unit order satisfies NU-001, as the reference code-point order does, and the two disagree on U+FFFF against U+10000: by code point U+FFFF precedes U+10000, by UTF-16 code unit U+10000 (the surrogate pair D800 DC00) precedes U+FFFF.
  <pre>NU_001 utf16NameImpl ∧ refNameImpl.lt "￿" "𐀀" ∧ utf16NameImpl.lt "𐀀" "￿"</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_forbids_shortlex` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ A shortlex order is rejected by line 5: on the ASCII names `"aa"` and `"b"` it puts `"b"` first, while code-point order puts `"aa"` first.
  <pre>¬NU_001 nu001Shortlex</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_mutant_astralTie` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Line 4 is load-bearing: the comparator that gives up outside the BMP keeps every other line (it is asymmetric, transitive and code-point order on BMP names) and is rejected, since neither of the different names `"𐀀"` and `"𐀁"` precedes the other, so the tie-break between them is undefined.
  <pre>NU_001_allBut 4 nu001AstralTie ∧ ¬NU_001 nu001AstralTie</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_mutant_cyclic` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Line 3 is load-bearing: the cyclic comparator keeps every other line (it is asymmetric, of two different names one precedes the other, and it is code-point order on BMP names) and is rejected, since `"𐀀"` precedes `"𐀁"`, `"𐀁"` precedes `"𐀂"` and `"𐀀"` does not precede `"𐀂"`.
  <pre>NU_001_allBut 3 nu001Cyclic ∧ ¬NU_001 nu001Cyclic</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_mutant_identityEq` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Line 1 is load-bearing (equal names for equal values): names compared by object identity keep every other line (the order is still code-point order) and are rejected, since two constructions of `"a"` are not one name, and a fork's siblings would never join.
  <pre>NU_001_allBut 1 nu001IdentityEq ∧ ¬NU_001 nu001IdentityEq</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_mutant_ignoreCase` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Line 1 is load-bearing (different names for different values): a case-insensitive name equality keeps every other line and is rejected, since `"A"` and `"a"` are different values with one name.
  <pre>NU_001_allBut 1 nu001IgnoreCase ∧ ¬NU_001 nu001IgnoreCase</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_mutant_nonStrict` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Line 2 is load-bearing: the non-strict order keeps every other line (it is transitive, total on different names and code-point order on BMP names) and is rejected, since the name `"𐀀"` (U+10000) precedes itself.
  <pre>NU_001_allBut 2 nu001NonStrict ∧ ¬NU_001 nu001NonStrict</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_mutant_reversed` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Line 5 is load-bearing: a reversed comparator keeps every other line (it is a strict total order) and is rejected, since on the ASCII names `"a"` and `"b"` it reverses code-point order, so the [NU-020] tie-break would pick the other name in every language that orders correctly.
  <pre>NU_001_allBut 5 nu001Reversed ∧ ¬NU_001 nu001Reversed</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): The test derivation on the reference: `NameId("a")` constructed twice gives one name, `NameId("a")` and `NameId("b")` are different names, and `NameId("a")` precedes `NameId("b")`.
  <pre>refNameImpl.eq (refNameImpl.ofValue "a") (refNameImpl.ofValue "a") ∧<br>  ¬refNameImpl.eq (refNameImpl.ofValue "a") (refNameImpl.ofValue "b") ∧<br>    refNameImpl.lt (refNameImpl.ofValue "a") (refNameImpl.ofValue "b")</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.clashNu_nameOrder` (Libpetri.Spec.ClashesNu): ✓ **nu-a#3, nu-b#5, ruling D31 (a).** Identical selection across languages is claimed for BMP names only, because the name order is a parameter. Worked example: Rust orders names by code point, Java and TypeScript by UTF-16 code unit. Both meet NU-001, the selection meets NU-022 at either order, and the two orders agree on every pair of BMP names. One correlated input holds U+FFFF and U+10000, both stamped 4: the code-point selection joins on U+FFFF, the UTF-16 one on U+10000 (whose surrogate pair D800 DC00 precedes FFFF).

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-NU_001_rename"></a>
## NU-001: Name Identity (renaming)

`Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_rename` · Kind **B** · Scope every executor; one firing of a transition with a match specification · Source **verbatim** (spec/12-nu-nets.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 6a5b71a3dce3b00b ai** · Statement hash `6a5b71a3dce3b00b`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| Whether a matched transition is enabled, and which tokens its firing consumes, *shall* depend on the names its keys project only through name **equality** and, for the tie-break of [NU-020], the name order.<br><br>*When* a matched transition fires with a chosen name, and a one-to-one renaming of names makes the renamed chosen name the chosen name ([NU-020], [NU-022]) of the same transition with every name its keys and relay targets project renamed, at the same marking, that renamed transition *shall* fire from that marking with the renamed chosen name, for the same emission, delivering the same tokens and leaving the same marking. | 1. For every transition t with match specification ms, every injective renaming σ of names, and every firing of t in R from M with chosen name n, delivery δ and emission e, leaving M': if σ n is the chosen name of nuRenameNames σ t at M (t with every name its keys and relay targets give renamed by σ; Selected over the selection input of t at M with every name renamed by σ, which is the renamed transition's own selection input), then R has a firing of nuRenameNames σ t from M with chosen name σ n, delivery δ and emission e, leaving M'. | <pre>fun {N V Nm} [DecidableEq N] [LinearOrder Nm] R ↦<br>  ∀ (t : NuTrans N (KeyFn V Nm)) (ms : MatchSpec N (KeyFn V Nm)),<br>    t.mspec = some ms →<br>      ∀ (σ : Nm → Nm),<br>        Function.Injective σ →<br>          ∀ (n : Nm) (δ : QDelivered N (Stamped V)) (e : List (N × Stamped V)),<br>            on fun M M' ↦ R t M (some n) δ e M', shall fun M M' ↦<br>              Selected (nuMapIn σ (matchIn ms t M)) (σ n) →<br>                R (nuRenameNames σ t) M (some (σ n)) δ e M'</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is a ν firing relation R over queue markings of stamped tokens (NuFireRel), as for NU_020_enable and NU_021: R t M c δ e M' says that t fires from M with chosen name c, delivers δ, the action emits e, and the firing leaves M'. A renaming of names is a function σ from names to names applied to what every key and relay target projects (nuRenameNames); the places, arcs, output spec, token values, markings and emissions are untouched, so 'the same transition with every name its keys and relay targets project renamed' is nuRenameNames σ t and token payloads are not renamed. It is injective because a renaming that merges two names changes name equality, which the sentence lets a firing read: a matcher whose name index folds names that differ, such as a case-folding NameId, is rejected (NU_001_rename_forbids_folded). 'Is enabled' and 'which tokens its firing consumes' are read as: the firing exists, with the same delivery and the same result.
- The name order enters only through the premise: σ n must be the chosen name of the renamed transition at M (Selected over the renamed selection input, which is the renamed transition's own selection input at M, nu001_matchIn_rename). The premise speaks of the renamed side only; that n is the chosen name of t at M is not assumed, and for a relation that meets NU_020_enable it holds anyway. A renaming that keeps the name order keeps the pick of every firing NU_020_enable allows, so with NU_020_enable the line gives 'a firing commutes with every strictly monotone renaming' (nu001_rename_strictMono). A renaming that does not keep the name order is what rules out reading the order anywhere but the tie-break: a matcher that fires only when the chosen name is the least name held in its correlated inputs meets every firing line of NU-020 and is rejected here (NU_001_rename_mutant_leastHeld), and so is a matcher that treats the name 0 as no name, a test on the content of a name (NU_001_rename_forbids_zeroAsNone, the case NU-021's assumes defers to this line).
- When the renaming changes which name the tie-break picks (possible only when two eligible names share their earliest createdAt), the line says nothing of the renamed transition's firing under the new pick. That it fires is the conjunct NuCovers of the ν consistency theorem: a transition enabled on its counts fires under its Selected name with every offered, relay-checked emission, and being enabled on the counts and eligibility read names only through equality (NU_020_enable's first two lines). So 'whether a matched transition is enabled' is this line together with NuCovers; enabledness is an existence clause and is not a line here. For a renaming that can be undone (a permutation of names) the line runs both ways when the pick is kept on both sides (nu001_rename_iff); a one-to-one renaming that is not onto has no one-to-one inverse, and for it the way back is again NuCovers with NU_020_enable's eligibility line.
- A firing whose chosen name is not eligible meets the premise under no renaming, since a one-to-one renaming keeps a name that is not eligible not eligible (nu021_eligible), so this line says nothing of it: a matcher that lets a reserved name such as the empty string join any name when no name is eligible meets this line and is rejected by the eligibility line of NU_020_enable (nu001_wildcard_left_to_NU_020). Rust, Java and TypeScript have no such fallback.
- The reference RefNuFire meets the line by NU-021's equivariance lemma refNuFire_transfer at the pairing 'equal values' (NU_001_rename_reference). The verifier's name symmetry is the same property one layer down: Route B's join enabling and steps are invariant under renamings (Novel.RouteB.joinEnab_inv, joinStep_sym, mintStep_sym) and its canonical key under permutations of name symbols (Novel.CanonicalKey.canonicalKey_comp).
- AC4 (a one-to-one renaming of the names a join's keys project, which makes the renamed chosen name the chosen name of the renamed join, does not change which tokens the join consumes or the marking it leaves) is this line, and the test derivation's renaming check is NU_001_rename_nonvacuous on the reference. No test in any language yet runs a join with its keys composed with a swap of names, so AC4 has no runtime test; it is recorded here as open. AC1 to AC3 are accounted for by the F block NU_001.
- The sentences 'A name (NameId) is an opaque correlation identity, constructed from an underlying string value.' and 'The name order exists solely for that tie-break and carries no domain meaning.' are this line's design text. Transitions without a match project no name, so the line speaks of matched transitions only; timing, priority and the firing pass are not in the model, as for NU-020.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_rename_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✓ RefNuFire satisfies the renaming line: by NU-021's equivariance lemma with values paired by equality, the renamed transition takes the same tokens for the renamed chosen name, accepts the same emission and leaves the same marking; and the tie-break picks the renamed chosen name, which is the premise.
  <pre>∀ {N V Nm : Type} [inst : DecidableEq N] [inst_1 : LinearOrder Nm],<br>  NU_001_rename RefNuFire</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_rename_forbids_folded` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Worked example. Place 0 holds 1@0 and place 1 holds 11@1, 1@2. A matcher that folds names to their last digit treats 11 as 1, joins on name 1 and takes 11@1 from place 1, the first token of its bucket. Swap the names 11 and 12: the tie-break still picks 1, but 12 folds to 2, so the matcher now takes 1@2 from place 1. The renaming line asks for the same tokens, so it rejects a name equality that is coarser than equality of names.
  <pre>¬NU_001_rename nu001_folded</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_rename_forbids_zeroAsNone` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Worked example. Place 0 holds 11@0 and place 1 holds 11@1 (the marking of NU-021's examples, here with the key that reads the name off the value), and a matcher that treats the name 0 as no name fires with name 11. Swap the names 11 and 0: the only name that can join is now 0, the tie-break picks it, and the matcher refuses to fire, so the renaming line fails.
  <pre>¬NU_001_rename (nu001_gated nu001_zeroAsNoneGate)</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_rename_mutant_leastHeld` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✗ Worked example. Place 0 holds 1@0, 2@1 and place 1 holds 1@2; only name 1 can join, and it is the least name held, so this matcher fires with 1. Swap the names 1 and 2: the only name that can join is now 2, so the tie-break picks it, but 2 is no longer the least name held (place 0 also holds a token named 1), and this matcher does not fire. It meets every firing line of NU-020, so only the renaming line rules out reading the name order outside the tie-break.
  <pre>nu001_nu020Lines nu001_leastHeld ∧ ¬NU_001_rename nu001_leastHeld</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_001_rename_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_001): ✓ Worked example. Place 0 holds 1@0, 2@1 and place 1 holds 2@2, 1@3, and the join fires with name 1, the name with the earlier token. Now swap the names 1 and 2, which reverses their order: name 2 now has the earlier token, so the tie-break picks it, and the renamed join fires with name 2, taking the same two tokens 1@0 and 1@3 and leaving the same marking.
  <pre>RefNuFire (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M (some 1)<br>    (nuDelivered nu020_ms (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M 1) []<br>    (qAppend (nuConsume nu020_ms (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M 1) []) ∧<br>  Selected<br>      (nuMapIn (nu001_swap 1 2) (matchIn nu020_ms (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M))<br>      2 ∧<br>    RefNuFire (nuRenameNames (nu001_swap 1 2) (nu020_join Card.one Card.one)) nu001_M<br>        (some 2) (nuDelivered nu020_ms (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M 1) []<br>        (qAppend (nuConsume nu020_ms (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M 1) []) ∧<br>      nuInputs nu020_ms (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M 1 0 = [nu020_tok 1 0] ∧<br>        nuInputs nu020_ms (nu020_join Card.one Card.one) nu001_M 1 1 = [nu020_tok 1 3]</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.joint_nu_sketch` (Libpetri.Spec.ConsistencyNu): ✓ Worked example of one model for the ν requirements. <a id="Libpetri-Spec-NU_010_classify"></a>
## NU-010: Fresh-Name Minting (declared mints in the fragment classifier)

`Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_classify` · Kind **F** · Scope the fragment classifier of every ν verifier · Source **verbatim** (spec/12-nu-nets.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 fd54872eff1e4beb ai** · Statement hash `fd54872eff1e4beb`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| The fragment classifier ([NU-051]) *shall* give the mint role only to a declared mint.<br><br>*If* a transition without a match specification has no input arc on a coloured place, writes a coloured place and is not a declared mint, *then* the fragment classifier *shall* give it no role.<br><br>*If* the timeout outcome of a transition writes a coloured place, *then* the fragment classifier *shall not* give it the mint role.<br><br>The fragment classifier *shall not* give the mint role to a transition that has a match specification or an input arc on a coloured place.<br><br>*If* a declared mint has no match specification, no input arc on a coloured place and no reset, read or inhibitor arc on a coloured place, puts on each branch exactly one token, and never a drained batch, into each coloured place the branch writes, writes a coloured place in some outcome and on timeout writes no coloured place, *then* the fragment classifier *shall* give it the mint role, in both BASE and EXTENDED.<br><br>*If* a transition without a match specification has no input arc on a coloured place and its timeout outcome writes a coloured place, *then* the fragment classifier *shall* give it no role. | 1. For every coloured set col, fragment mode, list of timeout writes tw and transition T:<br>2. C gives an undeclared T no mint role;<br>3. if T has no match keys, none of its input arcs is on a coloured place, some branch outcome of T deposits into a coloured place and T is not declared, C gives T no role;<br>4. if some timeout write of T is into a coloured place, C gives T no mint role, declared or not;<br>5. if C gives T the mint role, T has no match keys and none of its input arcs is on a coloured place;<br>6. if T is declared, has no match keys, no input arc on a coloured place and no reset, read or inhibitor arc on a coloured place, every branch puts one token and no drained batch into each coloured place it writes, some branch deposits into a coloured place and no timeout write is into a coloured place, C gives T the mint role;<br>7. if T has no match keys, none of its input arcs is on a coloured place, every timeout write of T is into a place some outcome of T deposits into, and some timeout write is into a coloured place, C gives T no role, declared or not. | **Assumptions**

- The model is one fragment classifier C, per transition, as the glossary term Fragment classifier reads it (GlossaryNuVer): from the coloured set, the mode, whether the transition is a declared mint, its timeout writes and the transition, a role or none. No role means the net falls back to the name-blind over-approximation ([NU-050]); Rust's classify returns no fragment as soon as one transition is refused (classify in rust/libpetri-verification/src/name_fragment.rs, its per-transition early returns). That step, from one transition with no role to the net leaving Route B, is the pipeline's, not the classifier's, and no block states it: the pipeline model (Verifier/Pipeline.lean) does not model Route B's entry. The witness refClassify is Novel.RouteB.classifyS. Whether a transition is declared ('by naming it as a mint transition on the verifier', or 'by its consuming a declared budget place ([NU-040])') is an input; the budget half is NU-040's line and the named half a line of the verifier pipeline (open); a name given to the verifier that is not a transition of the net is refused (AC6, NU_010_unknownMint in Spec/Req/NU_010_ac6.lean).
- 'Consumes' and 'without consuming one' are read as an input arc, the ColouredInputs of the glossary. A reset, read or inhibitor arc on a coloured place gives the transition no role at all (NU_051's fourth line), so the lines hold under either reading of reset arcs, and the fifth line asks for no such arc.
- The fourth line is the shape of a mint in the body ('read a transition as a **mint**, one that writes a fresh name'; a declared mint writes into each coloured place 'it writes without consuming one'): a matched join takes its name from its keys ([NU-020]) and a coloured consumer is NU-051's, so neither is ever a mint, even when the declaration names it (declared_mints declares every transition that consumes a declared budget place, a join taking a permit included). A classifier that tests the declaration before the match specification gives such a join the mint role under BASE, where no admission line of NU-054 speaks for it; the fourth line forbids it (NU_010_classify_mutant_joinMint_killed).
- The fifth line is the admission ('Declared, it is Proven by Route B' in AC4 rests on it), on NU-051's pattern for the consume role: without it a classifier that refuses every transition meets the other lines (NU_010_classify_forbids_never). Its conditions are those of the shipped classifier (Novel.RouteB.classifyT and classifyS; rust/libpetri-verification/src/name_fragment.rs classify, the produces_coloured branch): the arc rule and the branch rule are NU-051's ColouredTestArc and SingleColouredWrites, and the mode plays no part.
- 'A transition that writes a coloured place without consuming one and is not declared keeps the net off both routes, and the verifier answers through the name-blind over-approximation' is the second line for Route B. Its Route A half is Novel.RouteA.shipped_mint, cited by NU_010_routeA_mint: a Mint row of the shipped Route A plan is declared and its timeout writes no coloured place. No Route A classifier is abstracted here, as for NU-051.
- 'What the executor writes on timeout ([IO-013], [IO-014]) is never a mint, declared or not: a `ForwardInput` copies a consumed token, name included, and an `Out.Place` writes a unit token, which has no name' is the third line: a timeout write into a coloured place keeps the mint role away whatever it writes (TW.unit or TW.forward). The sixth line says what the transition gets instead when it has no match keys and no coloured input: no role, declared or not, as in every runtime (the produces_coloured branch of classify in rust/libpetri-verification/src/name_fragment.rs, typescript/src/verification/analysis/name-fragment.ts:306, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/analysis/NameFragment.java:444, each refusing a keyless writer with a coloured timeout write before the ordinary branch). The third line alone allows the ordinary role, whose name step is the identity (VER_012), so the name a timeout forward deposits would never reach the name layer: NU_010_classify_mutant_timeoutOrdinary_killed. A coloured consumer's and a join's timeout writes are NU-051's and NU-054's lines.
- The outcomes of a transition are Route B's rows (Novel.RouteB.NuTrans.rows: the action branches, then the timeout deposits, rust/libpetri-verification/src/branch_outcomes.rs outcomes), and the timeout writes are the separate argument tw (Rust timeout_writes), as in NU_051. A timeout write therefore lands in a place some row writes; the model takes rows and tw apart, so the sixth line asks it as a premise (every timeout write is into a place of some row). Without it a tw that names a place no row writes would reach the ordinary branch of classifyT, a pair no runtime builds.
- AC5 (t1 and t2 forward their requests into a and b on timeout, a join on a and b: placeBound(done, 0) is not Proven on either route, with t1 and t2 declared or with budget a declared budget place) is the third and sixth lines on the classifier (NU_010_classify_nonvacuous refuses a declared mint whose timeout writes a coloured place, and NU_010_classify_mutant_timeoutOrdinary_killed forbids reading it as ordinary, which the other five lines and NU-051 and NU-054 allow) and, for Route A, Novel.RouteA.Retro.forward_mint_refused; the verdict itself is stated by no block (kind Q: Rust rust/libpetri/tests/nu_mint_contract a_timeout_forward_into_a_match_key_is_never_a_mint, Java NuMintContractTest aTimeoutForwardIntoAMatchKeyIsNeverAMint_routeB and _routeA), and the false Proven the refusal prevents is Novel.RouteA.Retro.forward_mint_false_proven.
- 'A declared mint that is not a transition of the net MUST be refused, by a failure or an `Unknown`, with the same reason naming it at every entry point' and AC6 (a name given to the verifier as a mint transition that is not a transition of the net is refused with a reason naming it, and a name that is a transition is not refused with that reason) are the block NU_010_unknownMint (Spec/Req/NU_010_ac6.lean, nu.md skeptic S3): a call that names an unknown mint transition is refused, with the reason `declared mint transition 'x' not in the net (NU-010)` (unknown_mint_reason in rust/libpetri-verification/src/name_fragment.rs) unless a refusal that does not read the declaration comes first, and a call whose mint names are all transitions is not refused with that reason unless the same call with no mint named is. How each language and entry point fails (an exception, Unknown, a panic, a ValueError) is configuration (kind N), and 'the same way' is read as 'with the same reason text' (ruling D20). The report sentences ('The report of a verdict from either route names the transitions whose mint contract it assumes', and the pointer when Route B declines only for an undeclared writer, undeclared_mints_pointer in name_fragment.rs) are report lines (kind N) that no block states; Rust rust/libpetri/tests/nu_mint_contract a_copying_producer_is_not_read_as_a_mint_unless_declared checks the contract line, and rust/libpetri-verification/tests/mint_declarations a_route_b_decline_for_an_undeclared_mint_points_at_mint_transitions the pointer.
- AC4 is NU_010_contract's (a verdict line no block states, kind Q); its classifier halves are the first line (the stock fork() undeclared is never a mint) and the fifth (declared, it is a mint), both in NU_010_classify_nonvacuous.

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-NU_010_contract"></a>
## NU-010: Fresh-Name Minting (mint contract)

`Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_contract` · Kind **A** · Scope the action of every declared mint, as the ν verification routes assume it · Source **verbatim** (spec/12-nu-nets.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 71f124af5f453a48 ai** · Statement hash `71f124af5f453a48`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *When* a declared mint that has no input arc on a coloured place fires, every name it writes into a coloured place *shall* be a name it minted with `freshName()` in that firing.<br><br>*When* a declared mint that has no input arc on a coloured place fires, every name it writes into coloured places *shall* be one and the same name, whether in one place or in several. | 1. For one firing of a declared mint that has no input arc on a coloured place, let minted be the names its freshName() calls returned in that firing and wr c the names it writes into coloured place c:<br>2. every name written into a coloured place is in minted;<br>3. any two names written into coloured places, the same place or two places, are equal. | <pre>fun {C Nm} minted wr ↦<br>  (∀ (c : C), ∀ w ∈ wr c, w ∈ minted) ∧ ∀ (c c' : C), ∀ w ∈ wr c, ∀ w' ∈ wr c', w = w'</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The block is an assumption on the net author (kind A), not a behaviour of the executor: an action may write any value into a match key, a correlation id copied from its input included, and no analysis can tell a minting action from a copying one (the stock fork() action copies its input). No runtime checks it. The statement reads only what one firing minted and what it wrote into the coloured places, so it is a predicate on the action whatever executor runs it.
- Ruling D78 (a): one fresh name per firing, the same in every coloured place it writes, which is what the analyses assume. The per-place reading (a fresh name in each place, two places possibly getting two different names) is set aside: Reference.eachFresh_not_mintContract shows it is weaker, and NU_010_contract_forbids_twoNames that the second line rules it out. The second line also covers two tokens in ONE place ('whether in one place or in several'): a reading that compares only two different places allows two fresh names in one place, and NU_010_contract_mutant_otherPlaces_killed rules it out.
- The contract restricts what a firing writes and obliges no write: a firing that writes no coloured place keeps it ('Every name a declared mint writes ... MUST be ...' speaks of the names written). nu010_contract_fresh therefore asks, besides the contract, that the firing minted a name, so that MintContract has a name to give.
- What the assumption buys is nu010_contract_fresh: with the reference minter, a firing that keeps the contract writes a name held in no coloured place, whenever every held name was minted earlier in the run or under another scope of the restore lineage (NU-011). That is Reference.MintContract, and Reference.mintContract_iff_routeB makes it Novel.RouteB.Contract at Role.mint, the premise of Route B's soundness ([NU-050]). On the reference ν executor the contract both routes' runs keep is this MintContract too: NuLink.nuContract_mint_iff (Route B) and NuLinkA.nuContract_mint_iff (Route A), which NU_050_soundB and NU_050_soundA cite. The assumption is load-bearing: a declared mint that copies its input breaks the Route B simulation (Novel.RouteB.copyingMint_breaks_simulation).
- Which transitions are declared mints ('by naming it as a mint transition on the verifier (`mintTransitions` / `mint_transitions`)', or 'by its consuming a declared budget place ([NU-040])') is the declaration the verifier computes (declared_mints, rust/libpetri-verification/src/name_fragment.rs:135-152); the classifier takes it as an input (NU_010_classify), the budget half is NU-040's line, and the named half (the names given to the verifier are declared) is a line of the verifier pipeline (open); a name given to the verifier that is not a transition of the net is refused (AC6, NU_010_unknownMint in Spec/Req/NU_010_ac6.lean). 'into a coloured place ([NU-051], [NU-054]) it writes without consuming one': the scope of the block is a declared mint with no input arc on a coloured place, as both quoted sentences now say. A declared mint that consumes a coloured place, such as a matched join that takes a permit from a declared budget place and relays its chosen name (NU-054) to a coloured relay target, writes a name it did not mint, and the contract does not bind it: NU-040 declares every transition with an input arc on a budget place (rust/libpetri-verification/src/name_fragment.rs:140-152), but the classifier gives such a transition the join or consume role and never the mint role (NU_010_classify's fourth line), so no verdict reads it as a mint.
- AC2 (a fork that stamps both AND-branches with one minted name produces sibling tokens that a NU-020 join later correlates) is NU_010_contract_nonvacuous: the reference fork mints fork#s:0, writes it into places 1 and 2, keeps the contract, and the reference join on 1 and 2 then fires with that name and takes one token from each.
- AC4 (the stock fork() copies its input: placeBound(DONE, 0) is not Proven unless mA and mB are declared; declared, Route B proves it and the report names mA, mB under the mint contract) is a verdict and report line ([NU-050]) that no block states (kind Q): Rust rust/libpetri/tests/nu_mint_contract a_copying_producer_is_not_read_as_a_mint_unless_declared and Java NuMintContractTest aCopyingProducerIsNotReadAsAMintUnlessDeclared check it, and refNuEntry_declared (NU_010_ac6.lean) shows that the reference entry point leaves a declaration of real transitions to the routes; the counterexample to the undeclared reading is Novel.RouteB.copyingMint_breaks_simulation.

**Evidence**

- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_contract_forbids_copy` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example: the stock `fork()` copies the correlation id `7` it consumed into both places. It writes one name everywhere, but not a name it minted (`fork#s:0`), so the first line fails: the verifier would treat a copied id as fresh.
  <pre>¬NU_010_contract [mintName "fork" "s" 0] fun x ↦ ["7"]</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_contract_forbids_twoNames` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example (ruling D78): a fork that calls `freshName()` twice and writes `fork#s:0` into place A and `fork#s:1` into place B. Both names are fresh, but a join on A and B could never match them, and the analyses assume one name, so the second line fails.
  <pre>¬NU_010_contract [mintName "fork" "s" 0, mintName "fork" "s" 1] fun b ↦<br>    if b = true then [mintName "fork" "s" 0] else [mintName "fork" "s" 1]</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_contract_mutant_otherPlaces_killed` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example: a fork with ONE coloured output place calls `freshName()` twice and writes both names, `fork#s:0` and `fork#s:1`, into that place. Both names are fresh and no second place is written, so a reading that compares only two different places accepts it. The second line rules it out: the names of one place must be one name too.
  <pre>(NU_010_contract_mutant_otherPlaces [mintName "fork" "s" 0, mintName "fork" "s" 1] fun x ↦<br>    [mintName "fork" "s" 0, mintName "fork" "s" 1]) ∧<br>  ¬NU_010_contract [mintName "fork" "s" 0, mintName "fork" "s" 1] fun x ↦<br>      [mintName "fork" "s" 0, mintName "fork" "s" 1]</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_contract_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✓ Worked example (AC2). An executor with scope `s` fires the fork on one request. Its action calls `freshName()` once, gets `fork#s:0` from the reference minter, and writes it into both AND-branches, places 1 and 2: the firing keeps the contract. The reference join on places 1 and 2 then fires with that name and takes one sibling token from each branch.
  <pre>MintRun refMintSys (refMintSys.init "s") [MintEv.call "fork"] [mintName "fork" "s" 0] ∧<br>  RefNuFire nu010_fork nu010_M0 none (qDelivered nu010_M0 nu010_fork.base) nu010_e<br>      nu010_M1 ∧<br>    (NU_010_contract [mintName "fork" "s" 0] fun p ↦<br>        List.map Stamped.val (qEmittedTo nu010_e p)) ∧<br>      RefNuFire nu010_join nu010_M1 (some (mintName "fork" "s" 0))<br>          (nuDelivered nu010_jms nu010_join nu010_M1 (mintName "fork" "s" 0)) []<br>          (qAppend (nuConsume nu010_jms nu010_join nu010_M1 (mintName "fork" "s" 0)) []) ∧<br>        nuInputs nu010_jms nu010_join nu010_M1 (mintName "fork" "s" 0) 1 =<br>            [{ val := mintName "fork" "s" 0, stamp := 1 }] ∧<br>          nuInputs nu010_jms nu010_join nu010_M1 (mintName "fork" "s" 0) 2 =<br>            [{ val := mintName "fork" "s" 0, stamp := 1 }]</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.clashNu_mintOneFresh` (Libpetri.Spec.ClashesNu): ✓ **nu-a#8, ruling D78 (a).** A declared mint writes one fresh name per firing, the same in every coloured place it writes. Worked example: a fork that mints `fork#s:0` and writes it into two coloured places keeps NU-010's contract block. The contract the analyses assume is `MintContract` (one name, fresh at the marking, in every coloured place), which is Route B's `Contract .mint` exactly and implies the per-place reading `EachFresh` (every written name is fresh). A mint that writes name 1 into one coloured place and name 2 into another, both fresh, meets the per-place reading and not the contract, and a join on the two places could then never fire.
  <pre>(NU_010_contract ["fork#s:0"] fun x ↦ ["fork#s:0"]) ∧<br>  (∀ (co : List PlaceId) (T : Novel.RouteB.NuTrans) (M : Novel.RouteB.NM co) (n : ℕ)<br>      (hss : List (List ℕ)) (wr : Fin co.length → List ℕ),<br>      MintContract (fun i u ↦ M u i ≠ 0) wr ↔<br>        Novel.RouteB.Contract co Novel.RouteB.Role.mint T M n hss wr) ∧<br>    (∀ (holds : Bool → ℕ → Prop) (wr : Bool → List ℕ),<br>        MintContract holds wr → EachFresh holds wr) ∧<br>      (EachFresh (fun x x_1 ↦ False) fun b ↦ if b = true then [1] else [2]) ∧<br>        ¬MintContract (fun x x_1 ↦ False) fun b ↦ if b = true then [1] else [2]</pre>

<a id="Libpetri-Spec-NU_010_replay"></a>
## NU-010: Fresh-Name Minting (replay)

`Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_replay` · Kind **F** · Scope the minter every executor installs on the action context · Source **verbatim** (spec/12-nu-nets.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 9dffc6d46a47f3cc ai** · Statement hash `9dffc6d46a47f3cc`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| For a fixed scope and a fixed sequence of calling transitions, the executor *shall* return the same sequence of names to the `freshName()` calls, whichever firings the calls fall in. | 1. For every scope s and every two runs of Sy from its initial state for s whose calls come from the same transitions in the same order (the firing boundaries may fall anywhere), the two runs return the same names. | <pre>fun Sy ↦<br>  ∀ (s : String) (evs evs' : List MintEv) (xs ys : List String),<br>    calls evs = calls evs' →<br>      MintRun Sy (Sy.init s) evs xs → MintRun Sy (Sy.init s) evs' ys → xs = ys</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- Ruling D56 (a): replay is a MUST keyed on the scope and the order of the freshName() calls, not on the order of the firings. One counter per executor is read when the action calls the minter, so two minting actions in flight at once (a Rust async action runs under tokio::spawn, rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor_core/executor.rs:1679) may call it in either order; with one minting action in flight at a time, or synchronous actions only (executor_core/executor.rs:1491-1507), the call order is the firing order. Which order the calls come in is the executor's (RefExec), not the minter's, so the line needs no executor model. The sentence 'with one minting action in flight at a time the two orders agree, and actions that run concurrently may call the minter in either order' explains what the key means for the firings and adds no obligation.
- The line starts every run from the initial state for the scope. A restored execution is NU-011's: every runtime resumes under a new scope (NU_011_lineage, with the host assumption NU_011_host), and the other mechanism NU-011 names, a restored high-water mark, is used by no runtime and is outside NU_011_format. Replay of a restored execution is the replay of a run under its own scope, which this line covers.
- 'What replays is the sequence within a minting scope': the default scope is drawn at random per executor (NU-011), so a host that needs the whole name reproduced pins the scope, and a test compares names structurally. The line fixes the scope; the default scope and its randomness are NU-011's.
- AC3 (for a fixed sequence of calling transitions and a fixed scope, the sequence of minted names is reproducible) is the line. NU_010_replay_nonvacuous works it: [fork, fork] in one firing and [fork | fork] over two firings both return fork#s:0, fork#s:1. A minter that may return any unused name is unique but not reproducible (NU_010_replay_forbids_anyUnused, and NU_010_replay_mutant_uniqueOnly shows that uniqueness alone allows it); a counter that also moves at each firing boundary is unique and a function of its state, but keyed on the firings (NU_010_replay_forbids_boundaryTick).

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_replay_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✓ The reference minter satisfies the replay line: a run returns the reference names of its calls, whatever the firing boundaries.
  <pre>NU_010_replay refMintSys</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_replay_forbids_anyUnused` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example: a minter that may return any unused name. One call by `a` can return `p` in one run and `q` in another, so a replay of the same calls does not reproduce the names.
  <pre>¬NU_010_replay nu010_anyUnusedSys</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_replay_forbids_boundaryTick` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example: a counter that also moves at each firing boundary is unique and a function of its state, but keyed on the firings. Two calls by `fork` in one firing return `fork#s:0`, `fork#s:1`; the same calls over two firings return `fork#s:0`, `fork#s:2`.
  <pre>¬NU_010_replay nu010_tickSys</pre>
- ✗ **mutant** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_replay_mutant_uniqueOnly_killed` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example: uniqueness alone does not give replay. The any-unused minter never returns a name twice in a run, so it meets the uniqueness line, but the replay line rules it out.
  <pre>NU_010_replay_mutant_uniqueOnly nu010_anyUnusedSys ∧ ¬NU_010_replay nu010_anyUnusedSys</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_replay_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✓ Worked example (AC3). Under scope `s`, two calls by `fork` in one firing and the same two calls split over two firings both return `fork#s:0`, `fork#s:1`.
  <pre>MintRun refMintSys (refMintSys.init "s") [MintEv.call "fork", MintEv.call "fork"]<br>    ["fork#s:0", "fork#s:1"] ∧<br>  MintRun refMintSys (refMintSys.init "s")<br>    [MintEv.call "fork", MintEv.boundary, MintEv.call "fork"] ["fork#s:0", "fork#s:1"]</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.joint_nu_sketch` (Libpetri.Spec.ConsistencyNu): ✓ Worked example of one model for the ν requirements. On AC1's marking (branch A holds X, Y and branch B holds Y, X) the reference join is enabled on its counts and on names, the enablement check passes, the selection picks X (both names have a token at time 0, and X comes first in the name order), and the firing takes X from both branches; an action of the fork that calls `freshName()` is answered `fork#s:0` under the scope `s`; and the shipped classifier gives that fork the mint role when it is declared. One builder, one firing relation, one selection, one minter, one default draw and one classifier meet NU-020's four blocks, NU-022, NU-001 (both blocks), NU-021, NU-054's three blocks, CONC-008's ν-match block, NU-010's and NU-011's lines and NU-051's fragment lines, together with CORE-022, IO-011, EXEC-010, EXEC-012, CONC-004 and CONC-008, for every place type and token value type, with names in `String`; the agreement conjuncts tie each ν parameter to the one the other blocks use (the module docstring lists them). <a id="Libpetri-Spec-NU_010_unique"></a>
## NU-010: Fresh-Name Minting (uniqueness)

`Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_unique` · Kind **B** · Scope the minter every executor installs on the action context · Source **verbatim** (spec/12-nu-nets.md) · Sign-off **2026-11-13 fb41e4666108fdc8 ai** · Statement hash `fb41e4666108fdc8`

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| *When* an action calls `freshName()`, the executor *shall* return a name that differs from every name it returned earlier in the same execution, whether the earlier call came in the same firing or in an earlier one. | 1. Let Sy be a minting system (MintSys): a state, an initial state per scope, the mint relation of one freshName() call (state, calling transition, returned name, next state) and the step at a firing boundary.<br>2. For every scope s and every run of Sy from its initial state for s, a sequence of freshName() calls and firing boundaries in any interleaving, the names the calls return are pairwise distinct. | <pre>fun Sy ↦<br>  ∀ (s : String) (evs : List MintEv) (xs : List String),<br>    MintRun Sy (Sy.init s) evs xs → xs.Nodup</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is one minting system Sy, the minter of one executor. One execution is one run from the initial state for the executor's scope: a call returns a name and moves the state, a firing boundary moves the state by next. The reference refMintSys keeps the scope and ONE counter shared by every transition of the executor, starting at 0; a call by t returns t#scope:counter and advances the counter, and a firing boundary changes nothing. This is rust/libpetri-runtime/src/executor_core/executor.rs:180 and :203-217 (fresh_name_counter, fetch_add), java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/runtime/BitmapNetExecutor.java:1737-1739 and PrecompiledNetExecutor.java:436 and :465 (getAndIncrement), typescript/src/runtime/bitmap-net-executor.ts:1125-1126 and precompiled-net-executor.ts:1227. The state type is abstract, so a minter with a different state (NU-011's high-water mark) is a model too.
- Names minted by another execution, a restored one included, are NU-011's: the scope keeps them apart (NU_011). The name format t#scope:n and the scope check are NU-011's lines.
- The offer half ('A transition action MAY mint a fresh name via the action context'): every call is answered. A minter whose mint relation is empty meets this line vacuously, so the offer is the coverage conjunct MintTotal of the consistency theorem (refMintSys_total), not a line here.
- 'The executor installs the minter, one counter shared by all its transitions ([NU-011])': that the counter is one per executor, shared by every transition, is NU_011_format's last line (the i-th call, counting across all firings and transitions, returns t#s:i). A minter with one counter per transition that puts the transition into the name meets this line and the replay line, and NU_011_format rules it out. 'So the names follow the order of the freshName() calls, not the order of the firings' is the replay line.
- 'Absent an executor-installed minter, a fallback still guarantees uniqueness': which minter an action context uses when no executor installed one is configuration (kind N), and the fallback is not a line. Its uniqueness is cited by nu010_fallback_unique. The fallback is a process-wide counter that other action contexts may advance between two calls; Rust and TypeScript mint t#n (rust/libpetri-core/src/context.rs:204-212, typescript/src/core/transition-context.ts:19 and :308), Java mints t#<detached scope>:n (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/core/TransitionContext.java:488-497). The theorem shows that both formats give pairwise distinct names in every run, from any counter value. The fallback is not replay-stable, and the body does not claim it is.
- AC1 (two freshName() calls, within one firing or across firings, return unequal names) is the line. NU_010_unique_nonvacuous works it: two calls in one firing and one in the next return fork#s:0, fork#s:1 and fork#s:2. A counter reset at each firing boundary (NU_010_unique_forbids_resetPerFiring) and a counter per transition with the transition left out of the name (NU_010_unique_forbids_perTransition) are forbidden. The test derivation's three source tokens giving three distinct names is the same example; the join of each pair is NU_010_contract_nonvacuous.

**Evidence**

- ✓ **holds** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_unique_reference` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✓ The reference minter satisfies the uniqueness line: one counter per executor, read and advanced at every call, never reset, so no two calls of a run get one name.
  <pre>NU_010_unique refMintSys</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_unique_forbids_perTransition` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example: a counter per transition, with the transition left out of the name. The first call of `a` and the first call of `b` both get `s:0`.
  <pre>¬NU_010_unique nu010_perTransSys</pre>
- ✗ **forbids** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_unique_forbids_resetPerFiring` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✗ Worked example: a counter reset at each firing boundary. A fork that mints once in each of two firings gets `fork#s:0` both times, so two sibling groups would share a name and a join would mix them.
  <pre>¬NU_010_unique nu010_resetSys</pre>
- ✓ **nonvacuous** `Libpetri.Spec.NU_010_unique_nonvacuous` (Libpetri.Spec.Req.NU_010): ✓ Worked example (AC1). An executor with scope `s` runs a fork that calls `freshName()` twice in its first firing and once in its second. The reference minter returns `fork#s:0`, `fork#s:1` and `fork#s:2`: three different names, the two of one firing included.
  <pre>MintRun refMintSys (refMintSys.init "s") nu010_evs ["fork#s:0", "fork#s:1", "fork#s:2"] ∧<br>  ["fork#s:0", "fork#s:1", "fork#s:2"].Nodup</pre>
- ✓ **consistent** `Libpetri.Spec.joint_nu_sketch` (Libpetri.Spec.ConsistencyNu): ✓ Worked example of one model for the ν requirements. On AC1's marking (branch A holds X, Y and branch B holds Y, X) the reference join is enabled on its counts and on names, the enablement check passes, the selection picks X (both names have a token at time 0, and X comes first in the name order), and the firing takes X from both branches; an action of the fork that calls `freshName()` is answered `fork#s:0` under the scope `s`; and the shipped classifier gives that fork the mint role when it is declared. One builder, one firing relation, one selection, one minter, one default draw and one classifier meet NU-020's four blocks, NU-022, NU-001 (both blocks), NU-021, NU-054's three blocks, CONC-008's ν-match block, NU-010's and NU-011's lines and NU-051's fragment lines, together with CORE-022, IO-011, EXEC-010, EXEC-012, CONC-004 and CONC-008, for every place type and token value type, with names in `String`; the agreement conjuncts tie each ν parameter to the one the other blocks use (the module docstring lists them). The skeleton of `spec_consistent_nu`.

| Natural language | Plain reading | Lean statement |
|---|---|---|
| A declared mint that is not a transition of the net MUST be refused, by a failure or an `Unknown`, with the same reason naming it at every entry point (verification, script encoding ([VER-013]) and open-net verification ([VER-022])): `declared mint transition 'x' not in the net (NU-010)`, or `declared mint transitions 'a', 'b' not in the net (NU-010)` when several are not, each named once in code-point order.<br><br>A refusal that does not depend on the declaration, such as a stop before the call starts ([VER-013]) or an unresolved property place ([VER-003]), may come first, and that refusal is then the answer.<br><br>*If* a name given to the verifier as a mint transition is not a transition of the net, *then* verification, script encoding and open-net verification *shall* each refuse the request, by failing or by answering `Unknown`, and *shall not* answer `Proven` or `Violated` or return scripts.<br><br>*If* a name given to the verifier as a mint transition is not a transition of the net, *then* the reason of that refusal *shall* be `declared mint transition 'x' not in the net (NU-010)`, or `declared mint transitions 'a', 'b' not in the net (NU-010)` when several are not, naming each such name once and in code-point order, unless the same request with no mint transition named gets the same refusal.<br><br>*If* every name given to the verifier as a mint transition is a transition of the net, *then* verification, script encoding and open-net verification *shall not* refuse the request with the reason `declared mint transition 'x' not in the net (NU-010)` or `declared mint transitions 'a', 'b' not in the net (NU-010)`, whatever names it gives, unless the same request with no mint transition named gets the same refusal. | 1. Let E be an entry point, from a call c (solver, stop, options, net, property, initial marking, and the names c.mints given as mint transitions) to an answer: a verdict, the entry point's ordinary output (scripts), or a failure with a message. E c refuses with m when it fails with message m or answers Unknown with reason m.<br>2. For every call c such that some name of c.mints is not a transition name of c.net: E c refuses with some reason;<br>3. for every such c and reason m with which E c refuses: m is unknownMintReason of the transition names and c.mints, the text `declared mint transition 'x' not in the net (NU-010)` with each unknown name once, in code-point order, and `transitions` for several; or E answers the same call with no mint named exactly as it answers c;<br>4. for every call c such that every name of c.mints is a transition name of c.net, and every list of names xs: if E c refuses with unknownMintText xs, the NU-010 text naming xs, then E answers the same call with no mint named exactly as it answers c. | <pre>fun E ↦<br>  (∀ (c : MintCall), (∃ x ∈ c.mints, x ∉ callTNames c) → ∃ m, MintRefuses (E c) m) ∧<br>    (∀ (c : MintCall) (m : String),<br>        (∃ x ∈ c.mints, x ∉ callTNames c) →<br>          MintRefuses (E c) m →<br>            unknownMintReason (callTNames c) c.mints = some m ∨ E c.undeclared = E c) ∧<br>      ∀ (c : MintCall) (xs : List String),<br>        (∀ x ∈ c.mints, x ∈ callTNames c) →<br>          MintRefuses (E c) (unknownMintText xs) → E c.undeclared = E c</pre> |

**Assumptions**

- The model is one entry point E per call shape; verification, script encoding and open-net verification are three such E, and each meets the block with the one text function unknownMintReason, which is how the three are refused 'with the same reason' (ruling D20, nu-a NUA-10: 'the same way' was read as 'with the same reason text'). The mechanism is configuration (kind N) and the answer type folds it into a failure or an Unknown: Java throws IllegalArgumentException where the mint is declared, the open-net hook included (java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/smt/SmtVerifier.java:710-716, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/smt/opennet/OpenNetVerifier.java:80-81); TypeScript throws where it is declared on a verifier (typescript/src/verification/smt-verifier.ts:536-543) and open-net verification answers Unknown (typescript/src/verification/open-net/verify-open-net.ts:93, :188-189); Rust answers Unknown from verification (rust/libpetri-verification/src/smt_verifier.rs:780, :1201-1219) and open-net verification (rust/libpetri-verification/src/open_net/verify_open_net.rs:194-200, :332) and panics from script encoding (SmtVerifier::encode_scripts); Python raises ValueError from script encoding (rust/libpetri-py/src/verification.rs:949-955) and answers as Rust from verification. The text is built by unknown_mint_reason in rust/libpetri-verification/src/name_fragment.rs, java/src/main/java/org/libpetri/analysis/NameFragment.java:122-138 and typescript/src/verification/analysis/name-fragment.ts:96-102: the unknown names deduplicated, sorted in code-point order, each in single quotes, joined by ', ', 'transition' for one name and 'transitions' for several. Each builder gives no text when every declared name is a transition of the net it is handed (unknown_mint_reason returns None on an empty list), and every runtime hands it c.net or a net that keeps every transition of c.net (read as below), so the third line holds of every runtime by construction.
- Which names: the names given to the verifier (mintTransitions / mint_transitions, or a Java or TypeScript open-net configureSmt hook). A transition that consumes a declared budget place ([NU-040]) is declared too (declared_mints, name_fragment.rs:135-152), but it is a transition of the net by construction, so it never reaches this check. Java and TypeScript check each declaration call and throw at the first one that names an unknown transition, so the call's mints are the names declared up to that call; Rust checks the whole set when the entry point runs. Which net: c.net is the net the caller asks about: the caller's net for verification and script encoding, before any rewrite of the verifier's own, and the closed net for open-net verification, where all three runtimes check the declaration (verify_open_net.rs:194-200, verify-open-net.ts:93, OpenNetVerifier.java:80-81), so a name that only the closure adds, such as env:arrive[0]:p, is a transition of c.net there. Java and TypeScript check the caller's net at declaration (SmtVerifier.java:710-716, smt-verifier.ts:539) and TypeScript again in encodeScripts (smt-verifier.ts:1132, both on callerNet); Rust and Python script encoding check it too (encode_scripts, before with_arrivals; rust/libpetri-py/src/verification.rs:949-955), and so do Rust and Python verification: verify judges the declaration on the caller's net (smt_verifier.rs:780, before with_arrivals at :785) and verify_net answers that refusal before any route (:1201). The verifier's own rewrites, the Arrivals closure, the inert places, the in-flight split and the terminal rewrite, keep every transition of the caller's net and may add some, such as complete:t (completion_transition in in_flight.rs) or env:arrive?[0]:p under Arrivals(k) (close_arrivals in open_net/closure.rs, whose arrivals are all optional); a declaration of such a name is refused like any other name the caller's net lacks, at every entry point. An entry point that judged the rewritten net would accept it and answer a verdict, which breaks the first line; NU_010_unknownMint_forbids_rewrittenNet is that wrong entry point (the behaviour RD-38 recorded in spec/runtime-defects.md).
- Order of refusals: the second and third lines do not fix which refusal wins when the mint refusal meets one that does not depend on the declaration; they ask only that such a refusal be the answer the same call gets with no mint named. In Rust's verification the stop poll on entry ('net preparation', smt_verifier.rs:1146) and the unresolved property place refusal (smt_verifier.rs:1154) come before the mint check, and script encoding panics for a name-alignment property ([NU-055]) before it (encode_scripts); Java and TypeScript throw at declaration, so the mint refusal always comes first there. The reference refNuEntry follows Rust's order: the stop on entry, the unresolved place, the mint check, then the reference pipeline (pipeVerify). The lines read answers, so a refusal that came after the mint check but does not depend on the declaration also passes the second line; 'before any route runs' in the body (Rust) is the mechanism and not a line. The escape is needed: without it the second line rejects the reference, whose call that names frok and is cancelled before it starts gets the stop's reason (NU_010_unknownMint_escape_needed).
- What the block does not separate: the escapes accept any answer the same call with no mint named also gets, so an entry point that answers Unknown with one fixed reason to every call meets the block. The block tells a refusal for an unknown name, and the NU-010 text on a declaration of real transitions, from a refusal that does not depend on the declaration; it does not say that a declaration of real transitions leaves the verdict to the routes. That is AC4 ('Declared, it is Proven by Route B'), a verdict line that no block states (kind Q, NU_010.lean); refNuEntry_declared shows it for the reference.
- Out of scope: the report sentences ('The report of a verdict from either route names the transitions whose mint contract it assumes', and the pointer when Route B declines only for an undeclared writer, undeclared_mints_pointer in name_fragment.rs) are report text (kind Q). The open-net note that the graph was skipped, 'a declared mint transition is not in the net (NU-010)' (verify_open_net.rs:164, verify-open-net.ts:65), is a report note, not the reason; an entry point whose reason is that note is forbidden (NU_010_unknownMint_forbids_vague). Open-net verification has no reference entry point here: its call carries a contract that MintCall does not (Spec/Verifier/OpenNet.lean, close and judge), so it is covered only as a third abstract E; a reference open-net entry is an open item.
- AC6 ('A name given to the verifier as a mint transition that is not a transition of the net is refused, by a failure or an Unknown, with a reason naming it, unless a refusal that does not depend on the declaration is the answer; a name that is a transition of the net is not refused with that reason') is the three lines; its 'not refused with that reason' is the third line with its escape, since a refusal the same call with no mint named also gets does not come from the declaration. NU_010_unknownMint_nonvacuous works it on the net p0 -> t -> p1: the call that names frok is Unknown with `declared mint transition 'frok' not in the net (NU-010)`, the call that names z, frok, t and z again names frok and z once each, and script encoding fails with the same text; a call that names only t gets the reference verdict, Violated; a call cancelled before it starts gets `verification cancelled during net preparation`, as the same call with no mint named does.
